utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours. Events have occurred in the lives of some of us since we last met. In those in relation to this case, may I indicate two matters before Professor Wagenaar joins us. Your Honours, may I make it clear something which I think is already understood, that he is being called, as it were, on behalf on all three defendants. And the second matter which perhaps has not yet come to the attention of the Chamber, and certainly for my part it will considerably shorten matters. Your Honours have I think Professor Wagenaar's report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours will of course have read it and of course have appreciated that it is in three parts. It is only part 1 upon which we, the Defence, rely, that is to say that which deals with the Rules. Those two other parts that deal, if you like, with how those rules may be interpreted and/or applied as far as this case is concerned certainly seem to us who defend to be more appropriately and properly the subject of submissions in due course rather than evidence from Professor Wagenaar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So does that mean you only seek to rely on one part of the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes. It did not seem to us to be necessary to provide a supplemental amended report, because of course that's entirely a matter for Mr. Whiting, the ambit upon those matters which he cross-examines and that entirely of course is for him. But certainly, that which I propose to elicit in chief and that which we propose to rely upon are those matters that are contained in part 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honour, with those words in mind, with your leave, may I call Professor Wagenaar?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps before you do there are some lurking 92 bis statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And having reached the point of a draft decision only to find that the Prosecution response seemed to be conditional upon some agreed facts, the matter's been held in abeyance. And I wonder if really the two things are connected. Perhaps I will look at the other side --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Would you please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. I can see that your mind is not at this point. Yes. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just briefly address the point about the expert. It will be my intention only to question the expert on part 1 of the report, and that will of course shorten dramatically my cross-examination. If parts 2 and 3 had been introduced and relied upon in any way, I would have had substantial cross-examination in relation to those parts. Now, with respect to the 92 bis motion filed on behalf of Fatmir Limaj with regard to three statements. The agreed facts are connected to the statements and I can actually -- I have them here and would be happy to put them on the record and that would clear the way, as it were, for the Court's decision on the matter. And it will be apparent why the facts -- why they're conditional. If these facts had not been agreed, the Prosecution would have asked to cross-examination the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, Mr. Khan, is this a course that you're content with?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is. There is nothing controversial at all either in the 92 bis witness statements or in what my learned friend I anticipate is going to read out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. There are three statements which pertain to the three different 92 bis statements. The first one pertains to the RTK statement and the agreed statement is as follows --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Sorry, may I ask. Are these in a written form that we can follow?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: They're in a written form, but I only have one copy. So they're in a written form but you can't follow them because I only have one copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Proceed orally and you'll be able to let the court officer have a written form at the break. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's -- yes, I can do that and it's very short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The first statement is that: "Other political figures and former members of the KLA from Kosovo also appeared regularly on RTK from September 1999 onwards, including Hashim Thaqi, Jakup Krasniqi, Sylejman Selimi, Agim Ceku, Ramush Haradinaj, Rexhep Selimi and others. RTK also ran many stories about the war that included footage from the war and interviews with former KLA fighters." The second one is in reference to the newspaper 92 bis statement. "In addition to Epoka e re, other newspapers published in Kosovo are Koha Ditore and Bujku. Other political figures and former members of the KLA from Kosovo also appeared regularly in Epoka e re from the beginning of 2000 onwards including Hashim Thaqi, Jakup Krasniqi, Sylejman Selimi, Agim Ceku, Ramush Haradinaj, Rexhep Selimi and others. Epoka e re also had stories about the war that included photographs of former KLA fighters." And then finally with reference to the last statement from Dukagjini Printing Company: "Dukagjini Printing Company also provided printing services for other political figures in Kosovo, including Hashim Thaqi, Ramush Haradinaj, and others."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So those are the facts which are agreed, we understand, with the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And are put forward on that basis. Is that so, Mr. Khan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour. There is one very brief matter arising out of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can it be clear whether all accused agree with those facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry, Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, not at all. The Rules make provision under 92 bis for this procedure. Your Honour, we're totally in your hands. There doesn't appear -- well, there's no dispute between the parties as to the form of these statements. They are, as I said, very uncontroversial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're going to try and ask the Chamber to invent a rule that would allow you to avoid Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: No. Your Honour, of course Rule 92 bis is ex specialis, but of course it's subservient to 89 (C) and it appears to me in relation to costs and expedition there's no dispute between the parties. Matters can be, for example, read into evidence as my learned friend has done now. If you're minded to proceed with the 92 bis procedure, of course that can be done and, in fact, a formal request has been given last week to registry for the formalities to be started. But, Your Honour, if you were minded to admit these statements under 89(C), it might save the precious time of the registry as well as certain expenses to the Tribunal. But, Your Honours, it's a matter totally for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We're well aware, Mr. Khan, that in circumstances there is in essence agreement the Rules can be somewhat cumbersome. Nevertheless, the Appeals Chamber tends to require us not to ignore Rule 92 bis when we look at Rule 89. And in those circumstances, I'm afraid, our course must be to say that you should follow the procedures required by Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, that will be done. I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Unless of course you can get agreed facts. If you can manage that. It's a bit hard to convert a statement into agreed facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps we'll leave it as it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As foreshadowed, some other 92 bis --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: They're fast approaching. However, there is another matter that I would -- I'd like to attend to. I've been reminded that it should be taken care of which is if we could have the medical reports that were discussed in our last session which have been admitted be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Exhibit DB6?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Exhibit DB6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Should be received under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: DB6 would be under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think then we had better have the witness and Mr. Topolski can get underway. He's champing at the bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I'm completing my housework. May I inquire of Your Honours whether attached to Dr. Wagenaar's report you have the document headed the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984, Code D: Code of Practice For the Identification of Persons By Police Officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I see Her Honour nodding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I have two out of three.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just indicate it emerged in consultation with the professor this morning that he and I were looking at a different format of this document. If it turns out be the case, that is to say it differs from the one that you have, I now have spares here which would mean we all have the same. Would Your Honours indicate, should the need arise, if you're not following the pagination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Professor. Would you be kind enough to read aloud the affirmation that is on the card.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: While that is happening, I forget to indicate, Mr. Khan, that the three Rule 92 bis statements will now be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Does that mean that Your Honours' view of the professor is obscured?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We're blessed with a clear view of the professor and of you, Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Life can't get much better than this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Topolski:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, as you know, I appear together with Mr. Powles for Isak Musliu but you are called on behalf, as it were, of all three defendants. We're grateful for your attendance and assistance. May I, first of all, establish with you one or two preliminary matters before we get to your curriculum vitae. Before I do anything else at all, if I appear to you to speak more slowly than normal, it is on purpose. You'll appreciate that there are simultaneous translations going on. Would you be good enough to wait for my questions before answering them and I will try and wait for your answers to finish before the next question so the interpreter can keep up with us. Professor, is it right that you were first instructed in this matter on the 15th of April of this year?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We may need you to sit a little closer to the microphone. Thank you so much. Included in those instructions, Professor, were you sent what you were to describe as case files, materials in relation to this matter, which are set out I think at Annex A of your subsequent report?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were sent those I think, for the record, on the 18th of April of 2005. Is it right that you reported in writing and in detail on the 22nd of May of 2005?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it right that subsequent to that you had a number of discussions and meetings with members of the Defence teams?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last meeting you had, apart from today, with myself and Mr. Guy-Smith and Mr. Powles was a joint meeting between the Defence and Mr. Whiting, who I think was the only representative of the -- oh, no, there was another. Mr. Nicholls was there, I beg your pardon --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Somebody else was there as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Messrs. Whiting and Nicholls on behalf of the OTP, a joint meeting with Defence counsel, and that took place last week on the 24th of June?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, it's a long CV. May we seek to summarise it together. Can I ask you first to deal with your own education qualifications. Would you like me to remind you of them?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: No. Well, if you have a question about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Well, I can lead it from you I think. 1953 to 1960 you were at the Gymnasium in Utrecht?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 1960 to 1965 at the University of Utrecht where you took a doctorate in experimental psychology.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 1962 you took a doctorate in social sciences at Leiden University.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you are by trade and profession an experimental psychologist?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have been since the early 1960s been employed in a number of places and a number of institutions.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Including here in the Netherlands, of course, but in the early 1970s, you were visiting professor at Pennsylvania State University in the United States, where you were the recipient of a Fulbright scholarship.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You headed a psychology department at the Institute for Perception in Soesterberg, have I --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Soesterberg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the Netherlands, thank you, mid-1970s to mid-1980s. In 1982 to 1985, and I'm sure it is not a typing error, it is said that you were an extraordinary professor of experimental psychology

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: That is what it is called. You would now call it a part-time professor. I like the other title better.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm terribly tempted to say something but I won't. 1985 until the present day I think you enjoy the seat of professorship of experimental psychology at Leiden University.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have connections with a university in Belgium.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes, I had a special professorship at the University of Leuven.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're an permanent fellow of the Netherlands Institute for Advanced Studies in Wassenaar?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dean of University College, Utrecht?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: I have been that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Been that.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are an honorary university professor at Utrecht, and a professor of psychology and law at the Faculty of Law at Leiden University from 2004 until now.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've held a number of administrative positions, Professor, which are all set out in your curriculum vitae; I don't go into them. As far as honours are concerned, as we have established you received Fulbright scholarship in the early 1970s, other honours that you have had conferred upon you, including membership of the Royal Dutch Academy of Sciences and an overseas fellow of Churchill College, Cambridge, and not least, an honorary citizenship of Crete, are all honours that you have received through the 1980s and through the 1990s. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are the author and co-author of at least ten books on the subject of which you are to speak today. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A large number, perhaps in excess of 150 articles, papers written on the topic.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: On various topics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Various topics?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Not all on this topic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have in the Dutch jurisdiction, have you not, given evidence in a large number of trials?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And perhaps, if I may so, more relevantly for our purposes you have in fact appeared as a witness twice in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First -- in its very first case of Tadic. As you understand it, Professor, who called you as a witness in Tadic?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: I was first contacted by the Prosecution in Tadic and I worked with Mr. Alan Tieger at that time. And then the Defence also asked some questions and it was agreed I would answer questions of both parties simultaneously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Subsequent to that you gave evidence in the case of Kupreskic, did you not?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There you were called as a Defence witness?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, the report that we all have in front of us is split into three parts. And as you are aware, we only rely upon, and I say that of course with the utmost respects to parts 2 and 3, we only rely on part 1. Do you follow?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's only upon part 1 that I want to ask you a few questions and I apprehend Mr. Whiting will have some questions for you about it as well. May I deal with it this way, Professor, because we have all seen the report and the Tribunal has been good enough to indicate its redit. So it's going to profit no one to go through this line by line. It may be of assistance, and I'll stop if it isn't, if we as it were by way of headline only see if you and I can agree upon a headline notation, as it were, for each of the rules, because that's going to be the focus of the questions I and I think and Mr. Whiting will ask you. Annexed to the report is a document called the code of practice for the identification of persons by police officers. Is that correct? The English PACE zone 3/1:51 -

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- codes. Can I deal first with aims, Professor, aims of the rules. If one were to look at the code of practice, PACE codes, if one were to look at my page 128, the very first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I pause to see whether our pagination does correspond?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It might be 124 in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: 124 is the copy we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, then, can I hand up three clean sets, please. Does Mr. Whiting have it at 124 or 128? It's Code 1. I'm sorry it's not been stapled together. I should say the contents of course are exactly the same, it's just a different format. Same. Well, I'm going to do it by code paragraph number, not by page number. And I hope it will be followable, as it were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, Code 1 is of -- D is the introduction. Code 1.2 reads as follows, does it not: "Identification of witnesses arises, for example, if the offender is seen committing the crime and the witness is given an opportunity to identify the suspect in a video identification, identification parade, or similar procedure." These are the words I want to focus on: "The procedures are designed to test the witness's ability to identify the person they saw on a previous occasion and provide safeguards against mistaken identification." They are the aims of the code. Does that aim differ in any significant way to the aims of your rules?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: No, they are exactly the same aims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having dealt with the aim, therefore, can I move through the rules themselves. Again, Professor, attempting if we can, as it were, a shorthand description of each. And if there's anything that you briefly wish to add to the shorthand notation, please do, but bear in mind I know Mr. Whiting is going to be asking you questions about them. Rule 1: "The perpetrator must be unknown" is the first rule in summary form, is it not?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes. That is to say at the time of the crime the witness is should have seen the perpetrator not further known to him or her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Rule 2, insofar as it is possible, of course, there should be no prior sightings?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Not in between the crime and the test. Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Rule 3, again if one were to have a byline for this rule, could it be that the suspect should fit the description?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Rule 4, that when we are dealing, as we are here, with photo line-ups, insofar as it is possible, the foils should match the suspect?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes, and it's preferable that that's also tested before the photos are actually shown to witnesses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tested upon whom and by whom?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: So that -- as I described, that could be tested by a set of mock witnesses who are provided with a description of the crime and who come from the same population or ethnic group as the real witnesses. And if they are able, although they've never seen the criminal at the scene of the crime, if they are able to identify the one suspect in that line-up, then the suspect is said to be biased against that suspect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Rule 5, and here I want to cross-refer it, if I can, to something in the codes, the PACE codes. Rule 5 says, in essence, does it not, that witnesses should be properly instructed. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes. And there are some designs for standard instructions that can be used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we see where that - if the Tribunal does, it's a matter for them, of course - would have a mirror in the codes. Could I invite you and Their Honours to go to Annex E of the codes, which you might either find is on page 168 or 172, depending upon which bundle you're looking at. It's Annex E entitled "showing photographs."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: 168 in my copy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at paragraph 5, coincidentally and putting it beside your rule 5, does paragraph 5 of the annex to the code say this: "When the witness is shown the photographs, they shall be told the photograph of the person they saw may or may not be amongst them and if they cannot make a positive identification, they should say so. The witness should also be told they should not make a decision until they have viewed at least 12 photographs. The witness shall not be prompted or guided in any way but shall be left to make any selection without help"? Would you say, Professor, that that rule, that annex code mirrors your Rule 5?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah, although there are a few small differences. One is the number 12 --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh yes.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: -- which of course follows from another section in the code where it is specified that 12 is the proper number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: And the other thing is that in my description of the rules, a few aspects are added, like it should be absolutely clear to the witness that they may point at only one person. They cannot claim to recognise anyone if they recognise two or three people in that line-up. So it should be very clear that they can point at either no one or one person; there's no other possibility. My experience is that it helps to specify that in the rules.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Rule 6, although it goes entirely without saying, that the test you would suggest should include no suggestions and, in fact, should be conducted by someone independent. Can you define for Their Honours, please, who an independent person should be, in your view, to maximise the efficacy of this procedure, who that independent person should be.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: In fact, I did not use the word "independent" but I specified that the person who administers the test should not him or herself know who in the line-up is the suspect so that there is no way consciously or unconsciously to give away, to pass that information to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For example, in the United Kingdom, as I understand it, this procedure would be conducted by a police officer who has no connection whatsoever to the investigation, that -- such a person would qualify.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes. It would be very desirable to have such a person, but the essential thing is that this person doesn't know who in that line-up is the suspect. It might even happen that the police officer not connected to the case for one reason or the other has become aware of the identity of the suspect in that line-up. That should not happen; that is the essential part of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Rule 7 could be summarised, could it not, Professor, do you agree, as "all attempts by a witness should be reported and recorded"?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes, but maybe it's not so clear that this applies to two sets of identifications. One set are identifications concerning the same suspects, but it also applies to identifications that were made by the same witnesses, maybe for other suspects. Because if witnesses were either successful or unsuccessful at identifying other people, that would be highly relevant information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Rule 8 perhaps could be summarised by two words, "non-contamination." Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Rule 9 really deals with, as you describe it, various modes of investigation, if you like, in this respect. I wonder if one turned to find a mirror of this we might find it at paragraph 3.4 of the codes, which -- which is under the heading "cases when the suspect is known and available."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Really, what Rule 9 appears to be doing, Professor, is to set out, as it were, steps that may be available to an investigator in terms of identification evidence. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes. There is some sort of graded scale, one might say, an ordered scale of more- or less-desirable procedures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If one looks at the English code in 3.4, in the graded scale we do not see photo line-ups mentioned at all. Where, in your opinion, do such line-ups rank in the scale of effective and fair safeguarded procedures, Professor? Where do they rank?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Well, to begin with, there are two types of photographic identification procedures. One is in -- with -- one is that -- a procedure that uses photographs of the entire persons, from top to toe, often with some sort of a background with lines indicating the height of the people so that you can see whether they are tiny or big or tall or small. The second procedure is a procedure that uses faces, photographs of faces only, which tells you nothing about, say, the size of those people, or the posture of those people, or the build of those people, so that's limited to faces only. Obviously if the witnesses saw height and build and also describe height and build, it might be a good thing to use photographs that also show this so that the probability of correctly identifying or correctly not identifying such a person would be bigger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Rule 10 simply states "no dock IDs".

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Well, you can do that for administrative purposes, but it cannot replace a proper line-up procedure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to ask you one matter arising out of the next paragraph, that having completed a summary of the rules themselves, and then I have one only matter only to ask you about, Professor. The question you pose in the report between paragraphs 20 and 21 after Rule 10 on page 7 is what if the rules are violated. Now, of course you appreciate whether this Tribunal adopts any of these rules, first of all, and/or whether it finds, as a matter of evidence, any of those rules it adopts have been breached, it's entirely a matter for it. But do you have, Professor, an understanding of the way that the English courts deal with breaches of the codes? What do you understand to be the test that the English judge would apply when he or she is looking at the admissibility of identification evidence and considering whether there has been or was a breach of codes of the practice?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Although I'm not an expert in law and definitely not in English law, my understanding is that -- which of course is also sensible, that when you talk about violation of the rules, you do not talk about small deviation from the desirable rules, but you talk about serious and significant breaches of the rules which -- which to my mind implies that the probability of a false positive, a false positive identification is substantially increased, of course at the risk of the accused.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. A final question: Are you aware, first of all, of any criminal or quasi-criminal jurisdiction in the world that has adopted all or most of these ten rules, Professor?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Well, you have already referred to the PACE rules which of course in Europe is a brilliant example of qualification in an early stage even of such rules. In the Dutch jurisdiction, as I have noted in I think footnote number 1 of my report --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 4, footnote 1.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: The Minister of Justice has issued a decree that there are also rules for the Dutch jurisdiction which are laid down by the -- what's called the Recherche Advies Commissie, the criminal investigation advisory board, of which I was a member at the time, and in the handbook written by Mr. Von Amelsvoort for the police academy which is used by all police officers who perform such tests in our country. The decree of the minister in 2002 has its essential intention that the courts should test actual procedures being used in trials against these rules. And since there is not much difference between the rules from 1992 and the ones published by Mr. Von Amelsvoort in his textbook, the courts could choose either one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the Dutch national experience. Are you aware of any connection, as it were, closer to home, closer to this Tribunal and its investigating wing, as it were, as far as these rules are concerned?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Well, I've not seen rules for identification procedures, say, decreed by this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: But I've noticed a few things that I can give to you for what they're worth. One is that in the trial of Mr. Kupreskic, in the ruling of the Tribunal they explicitly underscored some of the rules that I presented then because they were particularly relevant in that case, and indeed decided not to use a certain piece of evidence that was brought forward then. The other thing that I can tell you is that - and of course you're all aware of this - that Mr. Von Amelsvoort -- that the handbook of Mr. Amelsvoort was translated by this Tribunal in English and then subsequently used as a textbook for the training of the investigators of this Tribunal. I think this happened in 1999. So I don't know exactly what officially that means, but at least it should mean that at that time it was thought -- it was decided that this set of rules would be very useful to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which year was this, Professor, as you understood it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: I think it was 1999 -- 1998 or 1999, but I think the Office of the Prosecutor can tell you more about it because I think they were more involved with it than I am. So they should absolutely be able to provide you with that translation and the details of this training.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'd just like to be clear precisely what your evidence is about it, please. Bearing in mind that we are dealing with a large organisation here.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which particular organisation within the ICTY do you say that these guidelines, these rules, were provided?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: I think I should not guess.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, you shouldn't.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: I talked to Mr. Von Amelsvoort who explained me exactly -- the reason I talked to him was to ask him whether there would be an English translation of his book to provide to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: And he answered they already have it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: That was when he explained that it was used in a training course for investigators - that's all he said and that's all I can tell you about it - investigators of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: No, I've not seen this document. I must also say that right now this book has its -- is in its fifth edition. The second edition was translated for this Tribunal but the differences are slight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I show you just for identifications purposes at the moment only a document, Professor, and ask you whether you've seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I'm very happy for Mr. Whiting to have a copy while I'm doing this. One for the witness, one for Mr. Whiting for the moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, just look at this document for a moment, will you, which is headed "guidelines For Multiple Photo Identification Procedure" and appears to have the name "Amelsvoort" at the bottom and a date in 1997. Have you seen this before?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: No, I've not seen this, but this seems to me, because I know the Dutch text, a translation of part of his handbook.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's your understanding, is it, that this or something like this is the material you've just been talking about that went, as it were, from Amelsvoort to the Office of the Prosecutor sometime in the late 1990s? Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to guess and I think there's no reason for me --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's why I'm doing it carefully and, I hope, fairly, Professor. If you can't say, then we can't take that any further. I don't know whether Mr. Whiting may or may not be able to help us.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: I can't say that this was the document used for training in this court. I can only say that this, to my understanding, is a translation of a section in Mr. Von Amelsvoort's handbook and it might well be it would have been a very useful basis to teach a course on, but I can't know whether this was the document used in that training.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. In those circumstances I take it no further and I have no more questions for you. Thank you. Would you wait there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Based on the position the Defence has taken, no questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Whiting:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Professor Wagenaar.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you know, my name is Alex Whiting and I am one of the members of the Prosecution team and, as Mr. Topolski said, we met, did we not, last Friday at your home. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I just want to repeat what Mr. Topolski said. We have to speak slowly. We also have to pause after each one of us speaks for the benefit of the interpreters. So after I ask my question, if you can pause before responding and I will try to pause before asking my next question. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I also want to make it clear that I'm only going to ask you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. questions about part 1 of the report. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, I would encourage you to focus on the questions and be as specific and brief as possible in your responses. With some luck, we can complete your testimony today. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Sure, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, of course if you need to respond at length to give a proper answer, of course you must do that.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: I will give you a warning then first.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, I want to start with the role of an expert in a case, and I want to ask you if you agree with this statement. And just so there's no mystery, it's actually from your own book, from the Ivan book from page 157. "There is considerable truth in the argument that the expert does not know which witness will tell the truth, but it is not the expert's task to make such assessments. The expert can only present information about variables that are possibly relevant. The actual assessment of witness reliability is in the domain of the court." Do you still agree with those words that you wrote?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to agree on some things just in the -- if we start to discuss some of these rules, I think many of the terms are clear in your report, but so that -- because sometimes there's variance in use of language in this area. The first is estimator variables and system variables. Now, these are words, terms, that you have used yourself in the articles. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: [No verbal response].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're nodding your head, but that doesn't get recorded on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, estimator variables are variables that are -- that in a witness identification that are -- occur at the time the witness sees the suspect, for example variables such as lighting, distance, exposure time, stress, things like that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And system variables are variables that are within the identification procedure; that is, some of the rules that you have been talking about, how many photos are shown, how you arrange the photos, who administers the test, and so forth. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those terms, were they first used by Gary Wells?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: They were introduced by Gary Wells, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Gary Wells, he is an expert who is similar to yourself, who works in the United States. Is that correct? When I say "similar to yourself" I mean --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: I don't work in the United States.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no, he works in the United States.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he say "similar to yourself," he works in the same area you do and in fact he takes many of the same positions you do on these issues. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: I know him as a researcher. I have no way of knowing whether he also studies cases or testifies in cases, actual cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, have you read his articles, some of his articles?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah, sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And have you seen in his articles that he discusses many of the same topics in this area?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he takes many of the same positions that you do on these topics?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you yourself, you've written about both estimator variables and system variables. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And while we have used two different terms for these topics, there is a relationship between the two; that is, that the system variables are created in some sense because of the estimator variables, that is -- let me try and put it this way: It is because of concerns about witnesses' ability to identify because of things like distance and time and stress that you create procedures such as the system variables. Do you understand what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, but now I need a slightly longer answer to that, because if you suggest that if the conditions of the first perception or the conditions for remembering the person that you saw are ideal, that in that case you do not need a special precaution with the system variables, then I would not agree. It's not so that if the estimator variables are perfect you may sort of fiddle with the system variables. If that's the intention of your question, I would disagree. I would say -- I would make a slightly different distinction than you do. Estimator variables are not under the control of the investigators; they happen at the scene of the crime or because of other conditions not under your control. The system variables are totally under control of the investigators, so that is their main responsibility. And rule-giving or even legislation, therefore, in the first place is applied to the system variables.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Just to press this point a little bit -- just a little bit further, do you understand that in some jurisdictions such as in the United Kingdom and in the United States that if a court has some concern about the system variables, that is the rules that were followed, what often is done is there's a look at the estimator variables to see, that is what the conditions of the identification were. Do you -- are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Well, in as far as it's at the discretion of the Court to accept or not accept identification evidence, not simply dictated by the fact whether or not rules were followed but just on the merits of the entire -- of the entire - how would I say that? - situation behind those investigations, in as far as that is at the discretion of the court, of course the court should also weigh the estimator variables to make such a decision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. If I could continue with the -- with just some terms so there's no confusion as we continue. A target-present line-up is a line-up where the suspect is present, correct? In a study. That's when the suspect -- when the suspect is present, you have a target-present line-up?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the suspect is absent you call it a --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: A target-absent line-up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, a foil is a photograph of a person who is not the suspect. It's sometimes called a filler or another term, but the term you use is foil. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah, but there's one more descriptive characteristic which is the foil is absolutely innocent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: If the witness points at the foil, we know that the witness is wrong.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A -- in a study, a hit, what's called a hit is an identification of the suspect.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: A hit is a positive, correct identification in the target-present line-up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A false alarm is an identification of someone who is not a suspect, that is an identification of a foil.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: It is an identification of a foil in a target-present line-up or an identification of a foil in a target-absent line-up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to move on to ask you about an estimator variable which is exposure time. Now, would you agree with me that most studies look at -- when they test witnesses, whether they be laboratory studies or real-world studies, generally they test exposure time of a matter of seconds, at most minutes. Is that correct? When you're describing most studies that are done in this area.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah, most studies reflect an actual situation, which is that most trials in which identification tests are used, that means in which the witness originally was confronted with an unfamiliar person. In most of these situations, the encounter in fact did not last much longer than a few seconds until a few minutes, and that is why also most studies reflect that situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at your -- the study that you did with others in 2003 on light and distance - and I appreciate that this was a study of recognitions as opposed to identifications --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- you described at one point in that study, and I have it available if you need to refer to it, that the faces in the study were viewed for a relatively long time." Do you recall that you used that description?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah, but now I must warn you that maybe there is an understanding -- a misunderstanding here. That study that you cite is on recognising familiar people, which means the first encounter -- say, one of these familiar people might be Bill Clinton, right? Now, the encounter with Bill Clinton might have been for hours on television, newspapers, whatever, only the test is described in this publication. But your earlier questions were about the length of the original confrontation. So you switched to another topic, which is all right with me, but I should at least --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I tried to be clear about that. I didn't want to be misleading about that. I tried to be clear about that by saying that this was recognitions as opposed to identifications --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I appreciate your further --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: But the confrontation was during the test, not at the scene of the crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. In any event, in that case the exposure in the second round was for 12 seconds in your study. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: That's say is the recognition test, which is -- in terms of identification tests the time that you spend at viewing each of the picture -- each of the pictures is in terms of so many seconds, not hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was 12 seconds in your study. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can move on to some examples of identification studies that were done. Are you familiar with a study that was done by Memon Hope and Bull in 2003?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: I think that's one that you submitted to me, right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I did provide it to you, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Let me see, because I'd like -- if you want me to comment on it I'd like to have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have it available.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah, I think I have it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Here. That's 2003 in the British Journal of Psychology. Right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah, I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have copies. It may be of some assistance to have this provided. The Defence and the witness have it, but it may aid the Court to have copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Just to make sure I have the right document, is that the one "Exposure Duration Effects on Eyewitness Accuracy and Confidence"?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Professor, this study reviewed previous studies that had been done on exposure time and found that the -- and just to be clear, this is with respect to identifications now, which is, as correctly stated, what I originally asked you about. This study reviewed the prior studies that had been done and found that the exposure time that had been examined in those prior studies ranged from - and this is at page 4 - ranged from 6 to 8 seconds to just over 12 minutes. That was the range of the prior studies. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in their own study what they did is they compared an exposure time of 12 seconds - this is at page 7 - 12 seconds to an exposure time of 45 seconds and made a comparison. And is it right that even in that -- in that comparison between the 12 seconds and the 45 seconds, it was found that there was a dramatic increase in correct identifications? I think --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Where do you find that conclusion? Maybe you can help me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I found it at page 17.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: 17? Because I seem to remember from this paper that there was a effect on confidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, there is also that. But if you look at page 17 in the second paragraph it says, I think it's the third -- fourth sentence it says: "There was a dramatic increase in hits from 32 per cent in the short exposure to 90 per cent with a longer exposure to the face."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: On page 17? Not in my copy, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is it titled "Discussion" at the top of... It's page 18, I apologise. I have a different pagination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I see what you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it that that conclusion does not particularly come as a surprise, that with longer exposure time there would be an increase in accuracy of identification.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm -- I agree with what you say about what they found. But there can be a confusion with respect to the words "identification." I'm not sure if they call it identification, and the danger is that you would apply such numbers on identification tests, as they are done in, say, criminal trials or criminal investigations. This is a -- what I would call a recognition study, so such high numbers as 90 per cent correct you should not, without further ado, I think, translate to a situation in a criminal investigation and draw the conclusion that after 45 seconds of exposure witnesses can identify 90 per cent of the suspects shown to them. With that understanding --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: I'm not saying that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm a little unclear because this is an identification study, not a recognition study; that is, that the participants were shown a video of a simulated robbery and then they were then shown photo spreads and asked to identify the suspect.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that then they were -- the two groups were compared. One saw -- had an exposure time to the suspect in the video of 12 seconds, one had an exposure time of 45 seconds, and the rates of hits, which we defined earlier, were compared. Is that your understanding of this study?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, you're absolutely right. But since you introduced the difference between estimated variables and system variables, I can easily point out to you that this study is on the influence of an estimator variable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Correct. But it's identification, not recognition. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah, we use the term -- I know the Tribunal uses identification and recognition in another manner as we in our --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm using --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: That's slightly confusing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm using the terms as you used them in your report.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: I used identification --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And recognition. You used those terms in your report. And this is an study of identification.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: I was trying to point out to you that this was a study on estimator variable with the system variables kept perfect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Understood. Understood.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm trying to focus on the estimator variable at the moment.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Which does not say very much about identifications in criminal investigations, where there might also be problems with the system variables.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's another subject which we may talk about later. But I'm trying to focus -- trying to isolate at the moment the estimator variables.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: You're absolutely right and the point I think confirms I think what I have said in my report, that if you use optimal procedures, identification can be highly reliable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the point is -- that's not the point I was trying to address -- trying to ask you about with the study. The point I'm trying to ask you about with this study is the effect of increased exposure time on accuracy of identifications. And it's fair to say that all things being equal, an increase in exposure time is going to lead to -- is -- correlates with increased accuracy in identification. Is that a statement you would agree with?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah, there's no doubt about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: If you would have asked what's the minimum exposure that you do need I would say 300 milliseconds. Above that it becomes quite good.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nonetheless, this study found a dramatic difference between 12 seconds to 45 seconds. Correct? Yes?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in your book the -- about the Ivan Demjanjuk trial, you talked about a study -- it's actually called -- what is fairly called a meta analysis done by Shapiro and Penrod --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- in 1986, and I take it since you have cited that in your book that's something that you're familiar with. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this -- what this study did is it analysed a number -- a significant number -- I think it's -- is it 190 studies that were done, and did an analysis of all the work -- of all of those studies and kind of put it together. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's what a meta analysis does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct that that study found a -- by looking at those studies -- and to be clear, I think only 8 of the 190 dealt with the issue of exposure time --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But looking at those eight studies that the Shapiro and Penrod studies found a correlation, what they said was an expected linear relationship between exposure duration and hit rates. Is that also accurate?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it that you are not aware of any study that studied exposure times in excess of 12 minutes or 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Depends on what you call a study. Of course there are cases described where people were exposed for days or years to other people and still misidentified them. But that's --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's -- so --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: So what do we call a study --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's talk, for instance, about laboratory studies.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Because in my report about the Demjanjuk case, also the Porta Debalus [phoen] case, where clearly his manservant who seen him for every day for a year identified the wrong person. So we're talking about a statistical relationship between exposure time and identification, which does not mean that exposure time is a guarantee for correct identification. But that's not what you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. And this business is all about statistics, isn't it, Professor? I mean, that's -- there -- all of these issues are about statistics. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Sure, but if you mean by statistics averages, I can't agree because statistics also deals with the outliers [sic].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But my point is there are no guarantees -- there are very few guarantees anywhere in this business. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is all about percentages and estimating and evaluating in terms of percentages.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah, some sort of statistics can be characterised like that and some sort of statistics deal with the range of things, the outliers in the worst cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just to get back to my question, to focus on the laboratory studies -- because it's fair to say that the laboratory studies comprise the overwhelming majority of studies done in this field, perhaps even over 90 per cent of studies done in this field are simulated laboratory studies. Looking at these simulated laboratory studies, you're not aware of a study which uses an exposure time of more than 12 or 15 minutes, are you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of the survey of experts in your field that was done by Kassin, Tubb, Hosch, Haas and Memon in 2001?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: That's about the number of statements, the number of -- the percentage of experts agreeing or disagreeing with certain statements?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Okay, let me... Yes, I'm familiar with that research.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you yourself participate --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Wait a minute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: You give me such a pile. I mislaid it --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I can provide it.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: But let's see whether we can deal with it. Oh, yeah, I got it -- no, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's just been provided to you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah, okay. I got it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you yourself participate in this survey?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: No, no. I think these are all American experts. As you may see -- well, I mean Memon is from Aberdeen but he did this when she was -- anyway -- no, I did not participate in this study.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Actually, if you look at -- and I hope it's the same pagination, page 3, look under the method in the second paragraph under the method under the experts you'll see that there were -- 53 per cent of the respondents were employed in the United States and the others came from the United Kingdom, Canada, Germany, Australia, the Netherlands. I thought perhaps that you were included?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, let's not rely on my memory for this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, dear. Now, this was a -- as we said, this was a survey of experts that was done in 2001, and it was to see whether there was agreement about certain propositions in this field. Is that a fair description of what this was?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you say -- would you agree that there was pretty widespread support for the notion that there is a correlation between exposure time and accuracy in identification? It's negatively expressed in this, that is the shorter duration, the less accurate the identification. But nonetheless, there's an agreement upwards of 85 per cent that agree with that proposition -- with that correlation?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah, I would say 81 per cent, but anyway. There is a problem with that research, as you are aware of, of course, because it very much depends on what exactly the question is that was asked to them. For instance, to give you an example, if I ask you: Do you think it would make a difference whether exposure time was half a second or one minute? Then all the experts would absolutely say yes, and I can testify about that. If you would ask: Would it make a difference whether exposure time would have been one minute or one and a half minutes? Then probably most experts would say, no, I don't think it makes much difference and I would not testify about it. So the question is: What exactly was the proposition? Were there any numbers mentioned?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if you -- I'll draw your attention --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Or was it just generally exposure time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could draw your attention to page 15. Were you familiar with this survey before it was provided to you last week?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So page 15, if you look at table 1, number 6, it appears that the proposition that was put --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- was: The less time an eye witness has to observe an event, the less well he or she will remember it.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: That illustrates my point. That's a very vague statement and the question is how the various experts would have interpreted this particular sentence, whether they would have said -- this question is about half a second versus one minute or is it about one minute versus one and a half minutes. And -- But I don't want to be -- I don't want to be difficult. I think exposure time is one of the important, if that's your point, one of the important estimator variables and of course exposure time is important for a court to know. And a short exposure time, a very short exposure time, makes it doubtful whether a witness had sufficient opportunity to see the criminal. And a long exposure time, combined with other favourable conditions like lighting, not wearing a mask and showing your face, and so on, is a very positive predictor of the ability to recognise a person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: If that's what you want to know, maybe we could go faster.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me before the break to put one further refinement on that, and that is in the first study that we looked at -- you can put that aside, I'm finished with that -- but the one that was done by Memon, Hope, and Bull, and I'm just going to put -- it's at -- it's my page 19 but it's probably your page 20. I think is it not that one on top there? Professor, it's being provided to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could draw your attention to page 20, I just want to see if --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 20.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want -- the authors of this study are analysing the results and they say at the top of the page there, they say: "The opportunity to view the culprit in a variety of poses and expressions may be more important than length of exposure. Changes in pose, expression, and details of appearance can significantly influence identification accuracy." Now, that is a -- that is a proposition that the authors of this study suggest in relation to their results. Is that something that you would agree with, that proposition -- that suggestion made by the authors?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: I think you should follow the discussion of this paper. See, one problem with exposure time is that you consistently find effects of exposure time, not always the same size of effect, and you do not find it in 100 per cent of these studies. And the problem they're discussing here is that if exposure time is just exposure to a stationary image that doesn't change, then it's probably not doing much. The effect of exposure time might be that a longer exposure time gives you, with moving persons, the opportunity to see that person from more angles. That's what they surmise here, that's the hypothesis. Now what do you ask me, whether I agree that that's a good hypothesis or whether I already have the answer to that hypothesis?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll put the question to you again and more precisely. Based on your experience and your work, do you -- have you found that any support for this hypothesis?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: No. In my own work I've never varied the number of angles in which you've seen the culprit, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So based on your own work you cannot offer anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: I can confirm that it's a sensible hypothesis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it makes sense to you, that is it seems that it would be correct.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: It makes sense that if you talk about real-life conditions and you've seen a criminal for minutes or even half an hour or an hour, then the fact that you've probably seen the criminal from many different angles will lead to a much richer storage of images in your memory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think perhaps a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. We must break now to enable the tapes to be changed. We will resume at 5 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Wagenaar, it's been suggested to me that we have violated at least one of the rules of the Tribunal, which is we are not pausing after question and answer and we are instead interrupting each other. So we have to try to be more disciplined. Could I turn, please, to paragraph 22 of your report. Do you have the report in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: I do. Paragraph 22?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 22.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in that paragraph you talk about certain cases where DNA has shown mistaken identification, and I want to draw your attention to the penultimate sentence on the page where you say: "In the survey published by the American Psychological Association Monitor, 1999, it is reported that 36 out of 40 wrongful convictions involved erroneous eyewitness identifications." Do you see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then the following sentence says: "Important shortcomings in the procedures were," and you list four different shortcomings.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are those -- are you suggesting in this paragraph that those four shortcomings occurred in these 36 of 40 cases? Is that how I'm to understand what you've written here? Or are you talking generally about shortcomings and procedures?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: I have this paper in front of me from the APA Monitor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe I could provide that to -- I have copies of that and if I could provide that to -- I think the Defence has, but if I could provide it to the Court. You're referring to the paper that you footnote in footnote 5 of your report. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this article by Scott Sleek is the source for what you've written in this article. Correct? You nodded your head yes, but if you could respond verbally.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, what the paper -- the paper discusses several things --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
