utterances.text: Well, Professor, you're going -- you're getting a little ahead of me. If we could take it one step at a time because you and I know about this but maybe not everybody. This paper -- this article, this three-page article is the source you cite for what you say here. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is the only source you relied on for this information about this study. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we could look at the source, at the first page it says in the fifth paragraph it talks about the study which reviewed 40 convictions and found that 36 involved eyewitness -- eyewitnesses identifying the wrong person. And that's what you say in your report, right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we could turn, please, to the second page -- and as you say -- before we turn to the second page, this article is not just about that study, it's also about other experiments and studies that have been done in this field. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: I was just going to say that when you stopped me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As I said, we have to take it one step at a time. So that's correct. This article is about other things, in addition -- not just about the study of 40 convictions, but about other matters. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Well, I would like to explain in my own words --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: -- what it is about. The article says: "In response to this number, the outcome of the DNA research, in the response, a group of psychologists, prosecutors, police, and Defence attorneys are prepared within the next several months to release a set of guidelines." To my understanding, then it says on page 2 at the bottom: "So far the group," so in response to these cases, which also includes psychologist Ronald Fisher have developed several recommendations. And then they made the following recommendations and then you get to the list of which I mentioned some of the issues in my report on the top of page 8 of my report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: So that's the connection between these recommendations, right, and the DNA cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Which is that a study -- a study group studied these cases and concluded that the following recommendations then are needed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- again, it's important to take this one step at a time. Not to belabour the point but to make it clear. The article on which you relied talks about other studies. For example, if you look at page 2, it's under polluted procedures it says: "Wells and other psychologists have offered the fallibility of eyewitness identification." Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Gary Wells is one of the people on this committee that's being talked about in the article. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Do we know that? I know that Ron Fisher was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if you look at page 1 it says at the bottom: "Psychologist Gary Wells, a member of the Department of Justice panel on eyewitness evidence. This is the panel that has been appointed by attorney general Janet Reno at the time."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Wait a minute. My page 1 says Gary was a member of the Department of Justice panel on eyewitness evidence. It doesn't say that he belongs to the study group instituted by attorney general Janet Reno.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're a aware that that's what it is, that Janet Reno appointed this group, the Justice Department panel on eye witness evidence, which then issued the recommendations?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: I can't tell whether they're different or the same. You may be correct, but I don't read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. If you look at page 2, it says that Reno appointed the working group in 1997.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So a considerable time before this article was written.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes, two years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's look at -- it says that recommendations that are going to be offered are these four things at the top of page 3. The officer working with the witness doesn't know which person is the subject, the eye witness understands that the person being sought for the crime might or might not be in the line-up, and these are the four things that you have written at the top of your page 8. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this article does not say that these were matters which were found in those -- in that study in those 36 cases, does it? Does it say that anywhere, Professor?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Well, it says that the working group in response to studying these cases came with the following recommendations. So logically I assume --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where does it say that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: On page 1 it says: "In response a group of psychologists, and so on, are prepared within the next several months to release a set of guidelines."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Uh-uh.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: And it's in response to these 40 convictions. So my supposition is that their work is based on those 40 cases and not on something else because if they were based on something else like the general literature or so, then I can only say there's nothing new in their recommendations because we've known these recommendations long before. The only new thing to me is that the study group of attorney general Janet Reno has found that especially these recommendations were important in the 40 cases. I may -- you may read it differently, but otherwise I can see no logical connection between the way the article starts with 40 false convictions reversed by DNA evidence and the recommendations. The only Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. connection can be that the study group instituted because of these 40 cases --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: -- came to the conclusion that these were important factors in these cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the inference that you've drawn from this article?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: That's the inference, otherwise the whole paper makes no sense to me. Because just saying that these recommendations are important is not worth having a study group for because we've known that long ago, like the first one, the officer working with the witness doesn't know which person is the suspect. I've written that in 1988 already. We don't need a working group instituted by the attorney general to come to that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, isn't it possible, Professor, isn't another fair reading of this article that this group was brought together because of cases such as these 36 out of 40, but that the recommendations that it's making are drawn from lots of sources, not just these 36 out of 40 cases, but from lots of sources, studies done and lots of information in the field. Isn't that also a fair reading and a sensible reading of this article?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah, we can speculate about other interpretations of this paper. I think if you want to know, you might well contact one of the authors, one of the participants of this group, but the way I read it is that these recommendations were inspired by looking at these 40 cases. That's the logic of this paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this be marked as an exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you mean that to be confined to that one document? This is the third you've put to the Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. This will be received.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Professor, there is a -- at the end of this article, it says -- at the very end it says -- it refers you --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document "Many Eyewitnesses Identified the Wrong Person" would be given Prosecution Exhibit 253.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, drawing your attention to the end of the document, there's in italicised type, there's a reference to -- for further information to the paper on the topic from the December 1998 issue of Law and Human Behaviour. Have you read that article?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: I think I need the specifics. I read Law and Human Behaviour; it's the leading journal, in your profession.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'll show you the article, maybe you'll recall it. It's entitled "Eyewitness Identification Procedures For Recommendations and Line-ups" --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah, it's in my collection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't want you to have to hunt around for it. I'll provide them to you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I provided this article to you last week as one of the articles I might ask you about.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you read it before I provided it to you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I just want to draw your attention to page 3. And do you see there's a table there, table 1, and it's a sample of 40 cases in which DNA evidence exonerated persons wrongfully convicted. And this is in fact a list of the 40 cases that are referred to in that study.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you'll see that in the very right-hand column it says how many identifications were in the case and if there was any other evidence. So, for example, for the first one there's a witness ID, third one it says: "Five witness IDs."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, would you -- I'm not going to go through the -- a laborious exercise of counting here, but there are 36, as has been reported, 36 of the 40 cases involved witness identification of some sort and 30 of those 36 involved a single witness identification. Would you accept that point?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And the dates also of the convictions are on this chart and I'll suggest that they range - you can check it - but they range from 1978 to 1991. Is that -- do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And these cases, as are described here, are all rapes, murders, violent crimes of that sort. Sexual assaults. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You can put that aside. We may come back to it at another point. Now, if -- can I turn, please, to paragraph 3 of your report. And I'm certainly not going to go over your qualifications, except I want to ask you about this point and it's at page 2, and it's something that we talked about when we met on Friday. It says: "Since 1985 I have served as an expert on questions of perception and memory in an average of 50 trials a year."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when we talked on Friday - and correct me if I'm wrong - but I think you explained to me that ten of those 50 involved trademark litigation.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: That's still on perception of memory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the 40 there were a number of cases that actually did not go to trial, where you consulted before charges were brought. Is that correct? And charges in some of those cases were never brought.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's included in the 40. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: I was consulted by the Office of the Prosecutor, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's included in your 40?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I've gone down to -- I'm talking now about criminal trials?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, you told me, as I understand, that you're on a committee that reviews all recovered memory cases in Holland and what -- before charges are brought?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Recovered memory cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I think I said. Yes, all recovered memory cases. And in some of those cases, charges are not brought. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in fact, in -- you provided us a list. In fact, in 2005 you were involved in -- so far you've been involved in four trials involving criminal -- four criminal trials involving identification. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Not counting this one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not -- this is number five. In 2004 there were six, and in 2003 there were also six. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So that's the number in those last three years, that's the number of trials -- criminal trials where you've been involved in identification issues. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on top of that in those years there may be a few more trademark trials, but certainly no more than ten each year.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, would it also -- with respect to the Tadic trial in which you testified, would it surprise you to learn that in the judgement you're described in paragraph 547 of the judgement as being a Defence expert. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: I'm not least not responsible for it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That wasn't the question.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: My position was very clear. I acted as an expert both from the Defence and for the Prosecution. In fact I was first contacted by the Prosecution and gracefully the Prosecution agreed that I would also answer questions by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: And how I am described by others I'm really not so much concerned with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that you were called to testify at the trial by the Defence? Are you -- were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: I probably would have been aware of it. I think it was in 1997, wasn't it? I don't really remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. I think it's 1996 --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: I won't disagree with you on that. You're the expert on legal matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I ask the question only because you suggested that you were an expert for both sides, and I just wanted to be clear on that point. That's the only reason I've put the question to you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: I was. I wrote my first report to the Prosecution, not to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. Now, turning to paragraphs 6 and 7 and 8 and 10 of your report --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Can you repeat where you're going? Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. 6, 7, 8, and 10. I'm going to try and --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Paragraph or page?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to go by paragraphs and I'm going to try and deal with those paragraphs as a group. They pertain really to Rule 1. You make a distinction, as you say, between recognition cases and identification cases.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: That's your terminology. That's the terminology of this Tribunal, which is quite confusing to the profession because we don't call it that way, anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whatever the terminology, the concepts represented by the terminology are certainly familiar ones in your profession. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: No, because we mean different things by identification and recognition than the Tribunal means. But I'm very happy to adopt the terminology the way it's used here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's use the terminology you've used in your report because that's all that's going into evidence in this case and that's what we have to talk about. Now, a recognition case is a case where the witness has seen the suspect before the crime occurs.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah, that's not the way I've used it in my report. For instance, on the top of page 4 you see that I say: "The recognition of an unfamiliar person," and that would be wrong according to your terminology because an unfamiliar person, according to you, cannot be recognised. You see, we use recognition as a term for psychological process, and identification as a term for a legal procedure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, would it be --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: You see?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be easier -- would it be easier if we used recognition of familiar person and recognition of an unfamiliar person?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah, but then we are a little bit at odds with the terminology in my report. As long as you're aware of that, it's okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm trying -- I'm trying to make this clear, so I'm trying to use the terminology in your report. Okay. So let's just say that -- let's say that a recognition case is a case where you knew the person beforehand --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or you'd seen the person beforehand and an identification case is a case where you never seen the person before the crime is committed?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Okay. That's the Tribunal's terminology.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please understand that is Mr. Whiting's terminology.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have no view yet; we are learning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, Your Honour, of course you are true and I'm simply -- I'm definitely not going to contradict you. But I've had a discussion with a different Chamber of the Tribunal before, so my impression is that you're very different -- the various Chambers are very consistent in using this terminology, that's why I said it's the Tribunal's terminology. But of course you're right, it's an inference on my side. It's the terminology that I've only heard within these walls, let me say that. But let's use the terminology because that might ease matters a lot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, before you do, Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I wonder if I could stir the pot a little further and invite caution, particularly on Mr. Whiting's part. At line 20 he's asking for a definition of a recognition case "where you knew the person beforehand." Answer: "Okay." "Or you'd seen the person beforehand as an identification case." So can we bear in mind that we need to stick to those and with those. Recognition is knowing the person, identification is seeing the person. Otherwise confusion will reign, I suspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I -- actually I think that's further confused the issue. The -- let's talk about -- a recognition is if you have ever seen the person before the crime is committed, whether you know them or you've just seen them, we'll call that a recognition case. Is that -- and I draw your attention to your first rule, which is in paragraph 10, where you say: "There should not even be a single occasion at which the witness might have seen the perpetrator before he encountered him at the scene of the crime." So that -- one category case is when the witness has seen the perpetrator before the commission of the crime.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: That's what I call familiar people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You call what?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Familiar people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. In that case, in those cases, it's your position that you do not use an identification procedure. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: No, not entirely. What I say is a multi-person line-up test in that case cannot prove the fact that the witness saw the suspect at the scene of the crime. I'm not talking about all identification procedures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's talk about multi-person identification procedures, whether they be a photo spread, a line-up or some other procedure.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Multi-person procedure. Your position is then that there is no reason to conduct such a procedure if the witness has seen the suspect before the commission of the crime.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: No, not really. I didn't talk about reason, I think. What I said is if you conduct a multi-person line-up in a situation where the witness might know the suspect from another occasion before the crime, then this multi-person identification test does not prove, cannot prove, that the witness saw the suspect at the scene of the crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: I'm not saying there's no reason to do it. I don't know what sort of reasons an investigator might have. I'm only saying such a multi-person line-up does not prove that particular point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't that the point of a multi-person identification test, in your view?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: That's why I would do it, but don't ask me about reasons investigators could have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But is there any other reason to conduct a multi-person identification test? Is there anything else that is accomplished, in your view, when the witness has seen the suspect before the commission of the crime? Does it accomplish anything, in your view?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Well, it's a quite laborious way to establish a few simple facts. For instance, I give you the example. If I claim that I saw in the middle of the night that my neighbour smashed my car window and stole my radio, then obviously placing my neighbour in a multi-person line-up with five or six unknown people would not constitute a difficult task for me. Of course I can point out who my neighbour is. It might help, that test, also it is somewhat laborious to make sure which neighbour I mean, right? Because I have many neighbours. So it's -- that assertance [sic] that it's this particular neighbour and they didn't arrest the wrong neighbour. It still doesn't prove that I saw him in the middle of the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to do that verification that you're talking about, the right neighbour, you don't need a multi-person test?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: I'm saying it would be a quite laborious way of doing it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You could just as easily and with the same result show one picture. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said absolutely?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah, but you asked me if there would be any other reason to conduct such a test and I said some investigators may do it in that way; I don't know of their reasons. I only say that such a test does not prove that I met the suspect at the scene of the crime. That's the only thing I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And -- and I side from --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: It's a matter of logic. It's only logic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'm just trying to pursue the logic here. Then therefore, as a matter of logic there is no reason that you can think of to show -- to use a multi-person identification test when the witness has seen the suspect before the commission of the crime?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah -- well, I don't know exactly why you're asking it. My experience is that in criminal trials I'm often confronted exactly with multi-person identification tests in a situation where the witness knew the suspect already before the crime. Apparently all these investigators saw reasons to do that and I cannot even start to guess what their reasons were. I do not think those tests prove their point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The only reason I'm asking you about this is it's your first rule. Your first rule says that there should not be a single occasion at which the witness might have seen the perpetrator.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that is your rule, and I'm not talking about what other investigators might think.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm trying to get your view on matters.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: I think we can easily agree on that rule because I think it is a very wise rule.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in a familiar-person case, when the witness has seen the suspect before the commission of the crime, then really the only issue is whether the witness had the ability, sufficient ability, to actually see the person during the commission of the crime and whether the witness is being honest.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Right. In a familiar-person case, the main question is estimator variables, if we come back to that terminology. Was a sufficiently favourable condition for the witness to see what he claims he saw? A multi-person identification test does not prove that point any further, so what you have to do is analyse the viewing conditions. And that's where it stops. If you want to believe that witness, you believe the witness but you cannot prove the truth of what the witness says by a further multi-person identification test.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to viewing conditions, that is a subject that you have written about in your -- I believe it's your 2004 article, which is entitled: "Familiar-face Recognition As a Function of Distance and Illumination, a Practical Tool For Use in the Courtroom."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes, and I talked about two estimator variables there, which is distance and illumination conditions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And with respect to those two estimator variables -- and you cite this article in your report.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to those two estimator variables, is it fair to say that you -- after doing your study, you come to the conclusion that recognitions of familiar faces that occur at a distance of less than 12 metres and at an illumination of 30 lux, l-u-x, which is translated in the article as being a badly illuminated room, that those two positions with those two estimator variables or better are reliable?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether I used the word reliable. I think I defined the quality of such perceptions in terms of diagnostic values and whether it's reliable or not, that's a rather subjective judgement. But what I said is that given a certain criterion value of diagnostic values for which I usually use 15, then in those conditions that you mention such diagnostic values can be obtained. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if I could -- if I could put --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: You may call it reliable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: I think I was slightly more exact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, why don't we look at the article; I have copies of it. Can I draw your attention to page 95. In that paragraph that starts: "Since the total diagnostic value," then it says four or five sentences into that paragraph it says: "Area 1 is defined by distances of no more than 12 metres and illumination values of 30 lux or more. Recognitions under these conditions can be said to be very reliable."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes, if diagnostic values are over 15.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yeah?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: It's part of the same sentence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's look at the last full paragraph on that page. "We concluded that recognitions in area 1, distance of no more than 12 metres and illumination level of 30 lux are reliable and recognitions in area 2 defined therein are questionable."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says, but of course you should keep in your mind that I'm really talking about diagnostic values.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document be given an exhibit number, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document "Familiar-Face Identification As a Function of Distance and Illumination, a Practical Tool For Use in the Courtroom" will be given Prosecution Exhibit P254.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just to the clear on this area of familiar-person cases, I just want to put an example to you and tell me -- ask you some questions to it. Let's say that a witness knows -- has a neighbour and knows the neighbour for a period of, let's say, a month and sees the neighbour every day, sees the neighbour in various conditions, has some conversations with the neighbour, does not know the neighbour's name. If the neighbour later committed a crime against the witness, under your rule number 1 you would not use a multi-person identification procedure.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: No. To me that would be a familiar person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All that you could do is have the person recount the circumstances of the crime and then you would have the person come and you'd have -- the court would have to test that person's honesty, correct, evaluate that person's honesty?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: No. The court then should look at what we have agreed to call the estimator variables, which is distance, illumination, amount of stress, and the number of things that you've listed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And of course evaluate whether the Court believes that the witness is telling the truth. That's of course --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: That's the ultimate question, I would say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And so there is no multi-person identification procedure that can be done to assist in the Court's evaluation of that scenario. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: It could be done, but it wouldn't prove the point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It wouldn't prove anything, according to you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move to --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Apart from the facts whether it's the right neighbour or the wrong neighbour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Which you've already told us could be done with a single photograph.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move to rule 2, paragraph 11. This is talking about an identification procedure in an unfamiliar-person case. And in this -- under Rule 2, if the witness sees the suspect after the commission of the crime, then a multi-person identification procedure also does not have any value, in your view.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Any logical value, because if then you test this person, the effect would be that you confront the person with one face or one picture of a person that looks familiar for at least one different reason and other people they've never seen before. So when the witness is able to indicate this one person, you don't know whether this is because the witness saw this person at the scene of the crime or because the witness saw this person at another occasion and looks familiar for that reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a matter of logic then, the -- an unfamiliar-person case where the witness sees the suspect after the commission of the crime becomes logically like a familiar-person case. That is, there's no logical reason to conduct a multi-person identification test, in your view?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's move to Rule 3, paragraph 13. You say in paragraph 13 that: "The suspect and all the others," meaning the foils?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Must fit the description given by the witness at an earlier occasion. If this description is in severe disagreement with the outer appearance of the suspect, it makes no sense to test whether the witness has an accurate memory of this suspect; we know he does not." Okay. What I want to get clear on is what exactly this description requirement means. Would you agree that when you're talking about this description requirement, what you are really focussing on is very broad categories, such as man/woman, white/black, very tall/very short. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: White/dark, long beard/no beard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. My next question was going to be that if there are discrepancies with regard to facial hair, height, weight, build, this would not prevent you from doing the test, would it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Well, depends. I said here: "The same holds for gross deviations with respect to age, posture, hair, facial air, specific marks." So with respect to facial hair if the witness says this person has a very conspicuous long beard and in fact you have a suspect of who it's known that he never had a beard and was, say, clean-shaven every day, then there is a -- I would say a gross deviation. If the discussion is about, if you do not shave for three weeks, do you describe that as unshaven or having a beard, right? Then you get in a grey area where it is not settled what you should. But I'm not talking about such an issue; I'm talking about gross deviations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What if the suspect is described as having a beard of some kind? Would it be a violation of this rule, in your view, to show photographs -- a photo spread with -- where all of the persons, including the suspect, did not have a beard?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Well, as I've said in my report, if you do that, you show the suspect without a beard, clean-shaven, and others, foils, without a beard, you transmit some new information to the witness. You tell the witness in that way, you described a beard, but actually the person you saw -- we believe the person you saw has no beard. And I'm always hesitant to present -- through the testing of someone's memory to present new information to that person's memory. Because what if next time, for instance after he's seen -- he's participated in this line-up procedure and he now testifies in this court, what if the next time he would argue, Well, in fact now I remember he had no beard. Did he change this testimony on the basis of re-finding his original memory or did he adapt his memory to something that he has learned in the line-up procedure? And it's my understanding that line-up procedures are not for giving witnesses additional information, they are for testing their memories.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it, in your view, invalidate the test? Put aside the issue of transmitting information. Would it, in your view, invalidate the test?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Well, you see, in some situations a test is weakened. You have weaker and stronger tests, and they can be so weak that in the end you would say, Well, this is not a valid test anymore. I would say that would weaken the test.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Ideally, in a test - and I think there's no doubt about it, say, in the various publications, even the publications that you have given me - that the people shown in line-up tests must meet, must conform to the descriptions given by the witness as much as is possible. And if it's not possible, yeah, then you can only weaken the test, if you still want to run it. But ideally that would not happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to show you the report that you wrote future Tadic case or one of the reports because you wrote several reports.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This became Exhibit D91 in the Tadic case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's a letter from you to Defence counsel dated 10 October 1996. And you recognise this letter, Professor Wagenaar?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a letter that you wrote?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I draw your attention, please, to paragraph 13. It's a little long, but I think it's worth reading. "One topic that recurred during the hearings of witnesses was Mr. Tadic's facial hair growth. It appeared that Mr. Tadic was sometimes clean-shaven, sometimes badly-shaven, and sometimes bearded. For the subjects who knew him well, this can hardly have been an obstacle to recognition, either at the scene of the crime or at later recognition tests because they were familiar with his various appearances. For the four subjects in group 2," and I'll just interrupt here. Those four subjects were unfamiliar persons. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "For the four subjects in group 2, there may have been a problem because the photograph used in the test shows Mr. Tadic only in one condition, more or less clean-shaven. If the person they saw commit a crime was bearded, they may have had a problem recognising him in the photographic line-up, but that is exactly the reason why the line-up is organised as a difficult test. If the beard problem formed a real obstacle, the witnesses would either not have indicated any picture or the wrong picture. The fact that all four witnesses identified the picture of Mr. Tadic indicates that the beard problem was not an obstacle to identification. The only exception is when the perpetrator was a look-alike of Mr. Tadic was this is not specifically related to the problem of facial hair. As stated before, multi-person identity parades, no matter how well they are organised, cannot exclude the possibility of a look-alike who is the true perpetrator. The beard problem is related to a more general problem of identity parades. The accused in the foils should conform to an earlier description of the perpetrator given by the witnesses." That's your rule. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: [No verbal response].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're nodding.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "I did not obtain a description of all four witnesses in group 2, nor am I certain that they were systematically collected. The general rule is that an identity parade should not be held when a witness's description is decisively different from the accused's appearance, such as when a small suspect is described as a remarkably tall person, a black suspect as a white person, a male suspect as a woman, a long-haired person as a bald person. The inclusion or omission of a beard and a moustache in this case is not such a decisive discrepancy." Do you still hold the view that you expressed in this -- section 13 of this report?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes, and I don't see a conflict with what we discussed before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: I've said a gross discrepancy would be a person with a remarkably long beard who's now without a beard. I've said a smaller problem -- where you only have a problem is where someone is badly shaven or has a -- a beard of two weeks or so and is now shown without a beard, that's only a problem, that's not the basic obstacle to running the test. But ideally, of course, you would present in the test the person who looks like the description. My criticism in this point 13 of this letter, and I hope you have noticed it, is not the way the pictures were presented but the fact that the earlier descriptions were absent. It makes it very difficult to decide where the pictures as used in the test were appropriate or not, and that's where my -- my judgement stops. If I don't have these descriptions, I can't comment on it anymore. So that's the point of point -- of item -- of section 13 is the fact that these prior descriptions were not provided.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you -- on this point in your testimony in the Tadic trial, didn't you say that if a photo -- a multi-person identification test, say a photo spread, is shown to a witness who described the suspect as having a beard and in the photo spread the person does not have a beard, then the test, if all of the persons do not have a beard, then the test will show whether the witness's perception was good enough or not, whether they are able to see through the beard.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: What I say here is that if the beard problem would have been an obstacle in the sense that witnesses might have recognised him with the beard but not without, then in fact since all four witnesses identified the picture of Mr. Tadic, you can't say the beard problem was an obstacle here. Right? But mind you, the quality of a test is not defined by the number of positive identifications only, it's also defined by the number of missed identifications. You don't want to set up a test in such a way that the likelihood that witnesses will not recognise a guilty person, that that likelihood is minimised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Professor Wagenaar --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: And if you picture -- if you picture the suspect in a way that it becomes very hard to recognise him, you might increase the probability of, say, a missed identification. That's not what I recommend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That -- okay. My only -- what I wanted to focus on because I suggest that you shifted to another topic. What I want to focus on is whether there is a problem in -- if the suspect is described as having a beard, whether there is a problem in showing -- using a photo spread where the suspect and the foils do not have a beard. My understanding is that if the perception is good enough at the time of the encounter, then a witness may be able to recognise the suspect without a beard, and the photo test, the line-up, has the -- the identification procedure has the potential to show that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes. But the diagnostic value is still reduced. You're saying a person might recognise the suspect in that case. Of course he might do that. What I'm saying is if it's possible to compose a line-up test with the suspect portrayed just exactly as he is described by the witness, that's to be preferred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's see how you express this in Tadic, and I'm going to provide you with the transcript of the first day of your testimony in Tadic. It's from the 24th of October, 1996. And if you could draw -- I'd like to draw your attention to page 5769 of the transcript. And specifically line 23 you say: "We have to distinguish between these two groups," and the two groups you're talking about is the familiar-person group and the unfamiliar-person group. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you go on to say: "The group who knew him already before with facial hair might not have had a problem because that is the face they were used to. Those who did not know him and saw him for the first time there and then with the beard, initially there is no problem. They do not recognise anything at that time, because that is their first perception of that person. Only later there is a problem, there might be a problem, because if the test presents someone without the facial hair, then they may not recognise him. But again, the test solves that problem; that is the beauty of it. If the perception was not good enough initially, they will not recognise him; they will fail the test. And we know it -- then we know it. If they recognised him in the test, apparently the perception was good enough; that is what the test proves."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you still hold that view? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes, but I would like to ask your attention for something you did not quote, which is on the same issue on the top of page -- the same page, 5769: "That reasoning holds only if the test is well performed," you see. You're describing a problem that originated in the estimated variables. Now, if you show a person that looks different in the test than the way he was perceived before at the scene of the crime but then you run a suggestive test, then the problem that is created by this discrepancy is easily overcome; that's what I say here. So the test will show whether this problem, facial hair or not facial hair, will lead to a nonrecognition. The beauty of that test exists only if the test is performed properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. I appreciate that point.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: That is the essential point, because if you have a suggestive test it really doesn't matter what they saw originally or who you show in the line-up. If the test is suggestive enough, you can always manage to let the witness point at one particular picture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, a suggestive test is a problem whether you have the beard issue or not. Correct? It's not only a problem if you have this beard issue; it's always a problem.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: It's always a problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: But in the case where there is a discrepancy between what they saw originally and what's presented to them in the test, if you want to resolve that problem, then the quality of the test really becomes critical. That becomes the decisive point. You see?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Staying focussed on this issue of description -- we've talked about beards. I want to talk a little bit about other descriptions, height, weight, build, things like that. Is it fair to say -- would you agree with me that people can know other people very well and be very capable of identifying their face and yet be incapable of providing an accurate description?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes, and there's even some research on that, of course. I myself, I think it was published in Dutch, always use what I call the rule of five. Five years, 5 kilos, 5 centimetres can always be -- you can always make a mistake of 5 kilos, five years, 5 centimetres. There's nothing to worry about. When it becomes substantially more, the question becomes whether the aspect of length, of age, of posture, of weight should not also be a part of the test. The problem, of course if you show only faces and there is a discrepancy of, say, 10 kilos in the weight description, you confront the situation -- you confront the witness with the situation where the witness cannot discover himself that something is wrong with the weight, and this cannot be the person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, you're jumping ahead there. We're going to talk about that later on. I'm just trying to focus on the description, not on the type of multi-person identification test that is conducted. You also have done an experiment, did you not, at your university where you -- you did an experiment with a class of a colleague of yours, a professor who had a -- quite a remarkable moustache, as you described it. And after a ten-week course where the students sat for two hours a week, you asked at the end for the students to describe the professor and you were struck by the fact that quite a few students missed the moustache.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you also aware that studies have been done which have shown that there is no relationship between a witness's ability to accurately describe somebody and their ability to identify a photograph of that person?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Sure, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: But, I must say, this is not about gross differences.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: The argument is not that people who describe a person as a black person would later be reliable witnesses in identifying a white person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: There must be something wrong there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Aside from those gross cases, very tall, very short, white/black, man/woman, you would agree that there is no relationship between a witness's ability to accurately describe a person and that person's ability to identify a person?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: If you talk about minute details, within the rule of five limits, then there is no relationship anymore. With the gross descriptions, of course there is a relationship.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You appreciate that there's quite a bit of distance between what you've described as the gross differences and the rule of five; there's a big middle area?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Sure, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And in that middle area you would also not be surprised, would you, to find individuals who may not accurately be able to describe somebody but who could very well identify that person. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Well, let me -- I know you think I'm jumping ahead, but the -- to me the meaning of this, if there are gross discrepancies between the description and our suspect, you do not even start to run a line-up test because you wouldn't know how to compose the line-up test. If it's within the rule-of-five type of discrepancies, there's no problem whatsoever. You can go ahead with constructing your line-up test, and in between there you have to think that it's quite possible that in between those two extreme conditions you think, Oh, okay, let the test tell us the truth. But that all depends on the quality of the test. Because in those situations if then subsequently you do not run the test properly, then you might go wrong. So there is all the more reason if there is some discrepancy in this, what we have called the grey area, to be very careful that you run the proper test so that you won't be misled in the end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I appreciate that answer. Are you also aware of studies which suggest that asking a witness to describe somebody verbally could later actually interfere with their ability to identify that person in a multi-person identification test?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah, that's called an overshadowing effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're aware of that --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That some support has been shown for that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Jonathan Schooler ran such experiments. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that if there is a discrepancy of the description of the -- provided by the witness and the suspect, that the foils should match the suspect and not the description provided by the witness. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Well, that depends on what sort of discrepancy we are talking about. See, there is always the requirement that the suspect should not stand out in the line-up from the foils. So clearly, if the suspect does not meet the descriptions and all the foils do, then the suspect would stand out; it would be an improper trial. So the logic would be that at least all the foils should look very similar to the suspect. If that means that in the end no one fits the prior description, you're running a rather funny test, especially when we're talking about gross discrepancies. I've seen a test, just to give you an example of how gross it can get, where a person describes a white culprit, and then he's confronted with a line-up of black people with the question of who of these black people is the white person you described? That doesn't make sense to me, and I think we'll easily agree on that. And the question is: How far on the road to such a strange confrontation can you go? When does it become meaningless? And that's a matter of judgement. Ideally, that problem should not arise. Ideally, the suspect should fit the prior descriptions and you have no problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But just to be clear, if there are minor discrepancies, then the most important thing is to match the foils to the suspect.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's move to paragraph 14, Rule 4, and this is matching of the suspect and the foils. We've already talked about this to a large degree. You say that it is necessary to do the and Test. Right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's what the report said -- what my report says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, that is not something that is required by the PACE rules which you have attached to your report, is it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, it -- we had talked before about this commission that was appointed by Janet Reno to come up with guidelines for the Department of Justice in the United States. Are you -- have you seen the guidelines that that committee came up with? Have you seen --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes, we've just looked at them. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before I provided them to you last week, had you seen them?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Are you aware that the Department of Justice in the United States guidelines also do not require that the Doob and Kirshenbaum Test be done. Okay?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you also say that the foils should belong to the same ethnic group as the suspect. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And that is also, as I understand it, not a requirement of the PACE rules or of the Department of Justice rules. Right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: No, it's not even in the Dutch rules.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: And as I told you, I become aware of that problem only in the Tadic trial. And subsequently when doing -- I did some research, as I told you, on the effect of different ethnic groups in the former Yugoslavia. And right now I'm running various experiments on other ethnic groups that might end up in the same line-up, unnoticed by those responsible for the line-up because they're not sensitive to this problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: And I think it's a real -- it's a real problem that especially emerges with investigators, prosecutors, Defence counsels, and judges all coming from the same ethnic group and not being sensitive to something which the witnesses may be sensitive who come from a different ethnic group. It's a real problem. You're quite right that it has not been realised until recently, so it did not end up in the formal rule. And what I say in point 14, because you made a quick shift there in citing me, I say: "It is necessary to establish that the test is not biased against the suspect." That is clear, and then I go on saying: "This is done in the so-called Doob and Kirshenbaum Test." I do not say it is necessary to do it through that test, there are many other ways, but it is at least necessary to make sure that the test is not biased. In the Dutch rules, translated for you as I mentioned before, in the Dutch rule it says not that you run a formal Doob and Kirshenbaum Test, but that you have two test observers who judge the fairness of the line-up, and that's the practice in the Netherlands that every line-up is tested by two independent test observers who are not familiar with the case. And I think that's a good procedure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: I still think the Doob and Kirshenbaum Test is an excellent manner of doing it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to the ethnic identity of the foils, you said: "It's a real problem." Wouldn't it be more accurate to say it's maybe a real problem, that it's a potential problem?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Well, I provided you with a list of cases in which I acted as expert on identification in the last three years. If you read the names of the suspects in those cases, you may realise why I said that because many of these names indicate people who came from different ethnic groups. And much of my testimony involved the problem of an unfair composition of line-ups, consisting of people from different ethnic groups. So it's -- that's why I call it a real problem. It's a problem in reality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it's a problem -- it's not a problem which has yet been demonstrated in studies, has it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Well, I demonstrated it for the people inhabiting the former Yugoslavia, together with my students Shara Lochun. I think that paper has also been copied for you because you asked for it. I demonstrated that there is a very real problem, and that as far as we could trace it, because it wasn't known, that the people composing the line-up of Tadic in fact had come from different ethnic groups. Now, what you will see, and that is I think clearly established in the PACE rules, is that the identity of the foils in line-ups should also be recorded so that we know who they are and if a discussion starts on are they from different ethnic backgrounds, that at least that question can be solved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: That's in the PACE rules and that is of course with this problem in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's -- let's look at the study that you provided regarding the former Yugoslavia. I have copies of it. And while this study's being distributed, it's fair to say that this is the only study that's been done on the former Yugoslavia, is that correct, that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: The only study that I'm aware of, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This study has not been published, has it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: It's a dissertation, and dissertations are, in principle, available.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But not published in any journal?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this was a study of possible stereotypes that people may or may not hold about people from the former Yugoslavia, number one; and number two, about different ethnic groups within the former Yugoslavia. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The study -- this did not study whether people from the former Yugoslavia or from outside the former Yugoslavia could actually distinguish by appearance between different ethnic groups within the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Could you kindly repeat that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. This study that -- you said -- this study focussed on stereotypes; it did not study whether people could actually distinguish in reality the ethnic identity of a -- an individual from the former Yugoslavia. Correct? It did not study that, did it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: But that's also not what you do in a Doob and Kirshenbaum Test.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just trying to get clear on what was studied and what was not studied. Okay. Now, this study had 26 people from the former Yugoslavia and 26 people from Holland participated in the study. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: As subjects. Not their faces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were the ones going through the tests. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Of the 26 people from the former Yugoslavia, seven identified themselves as Serbs, one as Hungarian, and 18 said they could not describe their ethnic origin. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So apparently no Albanians participated in the study?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Apparently --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apparently no Albanians participated in the study. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: They didn't tell us they were Albanians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nobody himself or herself as an Albanian?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: No, which doesn't exclude that in fact they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 52 subjects were asked to perform three tasks. The first was to look at a group of photos and say whether or not they thought the people in the photos were from the former Yugoslavia. They were not permitted to say, I cannot judge, I cannot tell. They were forced to choose. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If they thought that a person was from the former Yugoslavia, then they were asked to identify the ethnicity of the person, even if they had to guess. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, they were not allowed to say, I can't tell. They simply had to guess the -- take a guess at the ethnicity. Correct? Yes?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were then asked to provide descriptions based on a list of characteristics of their stereotypical image of the different ethnic groups in the former Yugoslavia. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So again, the study was not whether somebody could tell if somebody was Albanian, Serb, or Croat. Right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: No, and of course we couldn't do that because the identity of these people is not known.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. The people you were working -- the photographs you were working with, the identity was not known.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: These are people from the Tadic line-up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: And the commission was to study the possible misleading effects in that line-up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: So it's given that we don't know who these people are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it true that among the 26 people who participated in the study from the former Yugoslavia, it was found that their stereotypical images of Serbs and Albanians were in fact quite similar?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: It's also true that they had quite distinct stereotyped images of what typical people from those groups look like, and the whole point of this exercise is that if just by accident, just by accident, if the suspect is known to have come from a certain ethnic group, if just by accident the suspect appears to be one, the only one, or one of the few people shown to a witness who conformed to this stereotyped image, he will attract the attention. And in fact, a number of effective foils in the line-up becomes much smaller than you think it is. That's the danger of running an identification test with people who have come from different ethnic groups. They might conform or not conform to some stereotyped images and the only way to find out whether witnesses will recognise these stereotypes is run something like a Doob and Kirshenbaum Test; that's the excellent way of doing it. And in that way you can get a line-up that's neutral with respect to ethnic stereotypes and the test becomes more reliable. That's the only point. I'm not saying that people are able to recognise different ethnic groups; I'm saying that if only they have some stereotyped idea, then it could go wrong. It might be easier for you to understand. Let's assume we're looking for an Italian who committed a crime and now we place a person from the Netherlands who is not Italian but who's short and dark between others who are short and dark. The question is whether witnesses might now conclude, this must be the Italian we're looking for. You see? It's only the stereotype.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, Professor Wagenaar, in that example you would be able to look at the photo spread and see distinctions between the suspect and the foils or some of the foils. For example, you would see that the suspect was short and dark and the foils were Dutch-looking which is perhaps tall and blond.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that there are some ethnic groups that look different to people who are familiar with those ethnic groups but not familiar to us. So we cannot easily judge whether such a line-up just by looking at the pictures is a fair line-up or not. You can only ask witnesses who have experience with this group. To give you an example again, you might make a line-up with all sorts of Chinese people. Now, would a Chinese witness be sensitive to the difference between Chinese from the north or from the south or from Taiwan or even from Mongolia or maybe even a single Korean among them or Japanese? It's possible that we, all coming from the West, would not see there is something wrong in the line-up, whereas witnesses coming from that area would immediately see it. That's why I'm saying you need some sort of pre-test before you actually show a line-up to witnesses, you need a pre-test to make sure that this pre-test is not biased and that to the actual witnesses in fact some of the foils are not acceptable choices because they do not fit the description.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to take two points from this. Number one, you might expect that a Chinese person who could distinguish between the north and the south Chinese, for example, might be able to -- even though you would not perceive it initially, that witness or somebody else in that witness's shoes could point to differences that might be minor or overlooked by somebody who is not sensitive to them but which would still be visible. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what you mean. What I mean to say is that a line-up test should not be biased in this manner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what I'm trying to determine is whether these are invisible differences or they are visible differences which are not -- that the witness -- that the observer might not be sensitive to. Do you understand the distinction?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: It's quite possible that the witness, although he's sensitive to it, might not be able to express what the difference is --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you did --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: And unconsciously see that there is only one person who really comes from the group from which the actual culprit came. It's not certain at all that the witness that would perceive this would also be able to tell you this, hey, this line-up is no good, there is only one candidate in it. It's possible that the witness might not realise that, but through this suggestive composition be led to the one picture, pay all the attention to this picture, and then seem to recognise this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Perhaps this is a convenient time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. We must adjourn for the tapes again and resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, could the last study that was discussed, "Ethnic Bias and Identification Procedures" be given a number, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P255, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Wagenaar, moving on to Rule 5, paragraph 15, you state that: "Witnesses must be properly instructed," and specifically you say: "The instruction should explain to the witness that the wanted person may not be in the line-up." Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the -- the study that is most often cited in support of that rule is a study that was done by Malpass and Devine in 1981. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's one of the sources but not the only source.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's a study that, in fact, you have cited. Correct? Not in this report but in other places.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in that study, that study compared a group of people who were told that the perpetrator was in the line-up with a group of people who were told that the perpetrator may not be in the line-up. Correct? That's how that study was done.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.
