utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the danger of not telling a witness that the perpetrator may not be in the line-up is that the perpetrator -- is that the witness will assume the perpetrator is there and if the witness does not recognise the perpetrator will guess. Isn't that the --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- danger of not following that rule?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes, that is a danger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you have a fair line-up, those guesses will be evident. Correct? It will be evident they are guesses.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: If you have a fair line-up procedure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, a fair line-up procedure and a fair line-up --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: You said a fair line-up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: The line-up is just the composition of the photographs. The procedure is what the investigator does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You need both, a fair line-up and a fair line-up procedure.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: And a fair procedure. That's why I -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you have those two things, then the guesses will be evident. Correct? They will show up as guesses because they will be random.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: But if you combine -- just to finish your sentence. If you combine say an increased tendency to guess with something suggestive in the line-up or a suggestive behaviour on the part of the investigator, then the effect will be disastrous. And I also mention that I think in my report, it's the combination, the combination of weaknesses in the procedure that may lead to the wrong results; it's never just one problem, it's some defaults in the procedure combined with other defaults. And the wrong instruction is a very good candidate for combining with other factors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. That's very helpful. Let me -- let me read to you a sentence from your -- or a couple of sentences from your book "Identifying Ivan," which I have a copy of here if you need to refer to it. On page 50 -- and I think it illustrates this point that you've just been making. On page 50 you write: "In the previous paragraphs, I have demonstrated that the false identification of a suspect in a target-absent line-up is enhanced by the tendency towards making positive responses, but as explained in chapter 1, there is a second line of defence. Even when witnesses respond to target-absent line-ups, there is no special reason why they should point to the suspect instead of a foil."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: There ought not to be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Correct. There ought not to be?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: In a fair line-up, that is so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you also say in paragraph 15 that the question: Do you recognise any of these people? Is wrong. Now, isn't the only problem with that question that if somebody says, for example, in response to that question: I recognise the person in photograph 2, that you then have to ask follow-up questions such as: How do you recognise that person or from where do you recognise that person?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. This particular sentence is preceded by another sentence where it's explained that if the witness is confronted with a line-up in which there's only one suspect, but if that witness has described a number of perpetrators it should be made clear in the instruction to the witness for which of those perpetrators he is tested. So for instance, if he describes one as, say, the person who beat me, there were various people, there's one person who beat me up and he looked like this, then in the identification test it should be said, this test is testing the question whether in this line-up you recognise the person who you described as the one who beat you up. And then you give him the warnings that he may not be there and so on. So it should be clear in advance if the witnesses described various culprits for whom specifically they are tested now, otherwise -- and it's just a matter of I would say optimising the outcome of the test. Otherwise, you're making it very difficult for the witness and the likelihood that he doesn't know for whom to look makes the witness so uncertain that in the end he is not pointing at anyone. And the point of an identification test is not to let the witness fail. In fact the point of an identification test is of course to collect evidence against a possible really guilty person. So you should not design procedures in such a way that make it unlikely that the culprit will ever be recognised, so therefore you should be specific and tell them there's one person you described like this, do you recognise him, can you point him out, in this line-up or can't you? And that's why I add the question: Do you recognise any of these people? Is wrong. It should be: Do you recognise any of these people as the person you described as. It should be specific.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the danger of the more general question: Do you recognise any of these people, is that the witness may not be clear on what the task is and may fail, therefore, to recognise anybody?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah, or give you very confusing evidence. Like -- I'll give you an example which comes from the IRA murders in Roermond here which caused quite -- two Australian tourists were murdered here. There they were -- various people described by witnesses and they were confronted with several line-ups, but they were not told for which described perpetrator each of the line-ups was. So a witness said in line-up one, yeah, there I recognise, say, the tall gunman. And in the second he said, there I also recognised the tall gunman, which -- and it's quite possible in one of them he recognised them. But now you end up with a logical impossibility, evidence that cannot be used, just because the instructions were unclear and the witness had to guess what he should do. That's not helping anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some of those problems of course could be clarified by follow-up questions. Correct? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Quite often, no. Say, an identification is something you do and is a -- once you have said, I recognise that person, and then later on it must be turned back because he was looking for, say, the wrong person, you cannot turn it back. So you better get it right straight from the beginning and give them the proper instructions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you also say in this paragraph that: "A positive response should only be made in case of an immediate and certain recognition." Now, in your book "Identifying Ivan," you say, do you not, that it is firmly established, and this is your view, there's perhaps some controversy about it, but in your view "it is firmly established that confidence and identification accuracy are not closely related. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also say, at page 89, that "uncertainty itself is not a predictor of low accuracy."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So why then have a rule where only a certain response is acceptable?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Because witnesses, if they're not certain, say phrases like: This person looks familiar. I think I recognise this person but I don't know where I've seen him. Or This person I recognise for 70 per cent. And uncertain recognitions just ask for such statements, and it's very difficult to know what the court should do with such statements. So it is far better to tell the witness, Just point -- only point at someone if you're certain and your evidence is: I recognise this person with 100 per cent certainty; then we know what we're talking about. And I'm sure that with the uncertain recognitions, some of them might be correct. But if they are -- if these sentences are added to it, we don't know anymore what they mean. And in my experience, a recognition with full certainty may occur or will occur more often than you think, so you not exclude large numbers of recognitions that are now not counted anymore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But if --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: So there is no disadvantage in saying: Just respond if you're certain and only then, and don't tell us: I recognise him for 70 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, Professor, if confidence and accuracy are not correlated, as you say they are not, then isn't it -- then isn't it true that what you said about less-confident responses that witnesses might give could also be said about confident responses, that is that you can't be certain about what it means. Just because a witness says: I'm 100 per cent certain, how do you know any better what that means than I'm 80 per cent certain if there's no correlation between confidence and accuracy?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that a certain recognition is -- if the witness says: I'm 100 per cent certain that I recognise him, that the witness is 100 per cent of the time correct; I didn't say that. What I said is that uncertain responses with all sorts of qualifications make it extremely difficult to interpret what they mean. What does a person mean who says I -- this person looks familiar but I don't know where I've seen him. Well, the question is to identify a person he has seen at the scene of the crime and he described this person. Now he seems to -- someone looks familiar, but he doesn't look, apparently, similar to the one person he described. So why would that helpful, such points? It just raises questions and instructions should be proper. You should tell him, do not point to anyone who looks familiar; do point to someone who according to you, is the same person you described as so-and-so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, are you aware that Gary Wells, we've spoken about Gary Wells before, that he recommends that the instructions include an instruction that the witness state in his or her own words how certain he or she is of any identification?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: No, no. I think that's a confusing procedure. I've never recommended that. And in fact, I've never seen cases where a much more -- a stronger instruction has led a problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: No, I don't agree with that procedure. I think it's -- in principle it's inviting people to guess because you're telling them, if you're not certain, if you're only 70 per cent someone looks familiar but you don't know why, you may still respond. That means you're lowering the threshold of a positive response and that lowering of a threshold will also increase the number of false positives, and that's exactly what we don't want.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Professor, aren't those matters that are properly up to the court to evaluate, that is uncertain versus certain responses, to take that all into consideration when weighing the evidence?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Absolutely and they will have to, because I read in the transcript that some of those responses are of that kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But your rule would foreclose all but the certain responses.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: My rule if applied -- not faced the Court with such problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you're aware also that the PACE rules include a provision that if a person selects a photograph but is unable to confirm the identification, the person showing the photographs shall ask that witness how sure they are that the photograph they have indicated is the person saw on the specified earlier occasion.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. Now, what if the witness says I'm 70 per cent sure? What do we do with them or what do you do? I don't have to do anything. What does the Court do?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't that a matter for the Court?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: I think my task is to design a procedure, to advise about a procedure, that gives the Court as much certainty as is possible. I mean, I think therefore it's much better to tell witnesses, Only point as someone if you're certain. It's not only certain, it's also immediate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move to Rule 6, paragraph 16. You say that: "It is essential that the test be administered by an investigator who is not involved in the case." Now, I take it you are aware that this is a rule that is followed in some countries, for example, in the United Kingdom, is not followed in other countries; for example, is not followed in the United States as a matter of routine. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes, I am. I saw this was -- this was missing in the rules of the Department of Justice of the United States, and I was surprised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you would agree that if this rule is not followed, then it doesn't mean that there was suggestiveness, it just means that there was a possibility of suggestiveness. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: It also means that we cannot decide whether it has happened or not, whereas if the person who administers the test is simply not aware of the identity, that problem does not arise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you also agree that for suggestiveness to be a problem you need two components: You need suggestiveness on the part of the investigator and you need a witness who is susceptible to suggestiveness. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I want to read to you from page 153 of your book "Identifying Ivan" where you say -- and tell me if you still agree with this: "But in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. no way can the expert determine whether the witnesses were in fact influenced by the suggestive properties of the line-up. It is still possible that the witnesses recognise the suspect straightaway, that they would also have recognised the suspect if there had been no suggestion. The court can be told about the reliability of identifications in general, but it must decide itself whether it will accept the specific identification as reliable or not." Do you still agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's a case where suggestiveness is actually present in the line-up?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah, but I'm not advocating that the person who conducts the test should be aware of the identity of the suspect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that's clear.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: I'm only saying if he is aware, then something is happening that can only be evaluated by the court and we don't know how they should do that but then they must do that. They have an extra problem. Whereas if you follow Rule 6, then the court doesn't have that problem because that sort of suggestion simply cannot have happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move to Rule 7, paragraph 17, where you say that "all attempts at identification, including negative ones, must be reported." Now, you would agree, I take it that while all identification attempts, whether successful or not or positive or negative, must be reported and disclosed to the defence, that it does not follow that you can just add up the score and come out with a result. Right? You cannot just say, for example, Well, here we had seven out of ten identifications; therefore that's reliable, whereas seven out of 15 is not an acceptable number. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: There's no rule for determining the number of positive identifications that you need. There is another rule saying if you have a negative identification, at least there should be some explanation why that has happened. You cannot simply ignore the negative one and say, Well, we have enough positive ones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The court has to look at all the circumstances of the positive identifications and the negative identifications --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: And the negative, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- and consider all of the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah, it's quite possible that you have a negative identification and that you understand why that has happened and that it doesn't -- it doesn't harm, it doesn't mean anything for the positive ones. There are also conditions where there is a negative identification by someone who was in an eminent position to view the culprit and if he just says positively, Well, the man I saw is not in this line-up, well that's a very significant statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you would have to take into account not just the person's ability to view or their stated ability to view, but all other factors with relation to that.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Everything that happened in the meantime --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that witness's attitude and that --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Absolutely. But negative -- negative results of a line-up test are in principle as meaningful as positive ones. And if you want to accept the positive ones as evidence, at least you should be concerned about understanding where the negative ones have come from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's the court's job?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now -- but again, the numbers themselves don't tell you very much without knowing all of the circumstances. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: The numbers -- it's not -- it's not a voting game. It's not 5 against 4, so the 5 win or something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move to paragraph 18, Rule number 8 where you say: "Witnesses are not allowed to transfer any information about line-ups to other potential witnesses." Now, this is an example of one of those rules, is it not, where if you have a fair line-up procedure and fair line-up, that this rule -- a violation of this rule or a potential violation of this rule may not be so significant?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah. And I expressly said "if that is not practically feasible," because it cannot always be done. At least I think you can request that the best possible measures are taken. So if it's not possible to separate witnesses for a long period, at least you should tell them that they should not discuss the line-up; that's one thing. Another thing is, very simple, that if you have -- if you present several witnesses with this -- in principle, the same selection of pictures, you may rotate the positions of where the persons are located on that line-up. So that communication, Well, I saw him, he was in the top row, might not be helpful to the next witness. You may even envisage that if you have a new witness you find new foils. So there are lots of precautions you can take if it can be understood that the witnesses are in contact with one another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But just to get back to my question: If you are faced with that situation and you take precautions and you have otherwise a fair procedure and a fair test, then a violation of this rule may not be so significant. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: It is thinkable that this rule is violated and it does not lead to the conclusion that the identification test is therefore not valid and should be nullified, yeah. It's possible that this cannot be prevented. The least a court should do is get -- be informed about such things and then evaluate itself what it means to them; that's all you can do about it. But very explicitly I added here, which I did not with many of the other rules, I added the sentence "if it is not practically feasible" because, I agree with you, it is not always possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where it's not possible, then if things otherwise --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Then at least you can take some precautions and for the rest it's up to the court to decide how important that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your own view is that a violation of that rule may not be so significant in isolation? This is one of those rules in isolation.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah, if you took all the precautions, then the effect of it is also is diminished because then the information -- although the information -- if one witness says, I took part in an identification. He was there, I saw him. That's of course information that may convince the next witness that in fact the person who looks most like the person he remembers, that's him. And the warning in this instruction may be the person is not in the line-up at all, may not be effective anymore. So if it's possible, he should prevent those contacts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. And of course in that scenario that you just described, if everything else was fair, a random guess by the witness would show up on the test. That would be revealed by a correctly done test.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: If the test is run properly and only the threshold to give a positive response is lowered but nothing else, then you would still know it; that's the beauty of the test. But combined with other factors, this again -- this is especially harmful in combination with other factors. In itself, it might not be so harmful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's move to paragraph 19, Rule number 9, and you set out the different options. And here today you described this as a kind of scale of options with respect to a line-up, an identity parade, or a photo-spread procedure. Now, isn't it true that recognition of an individual is almost always entirely done by recognising the face?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Well, you are of course aware of the fact that there is some research on, say, the diagnostic value of these various forms of tests, where a test in which you see as much of the person as you experienced, say, during the encounter at the scene of the crime, and that might involve seeing the face from different angles, seeing how his face moves, hearing him speak, seeing how he moves, how he limps, or whatever. All those things may add -- and I only said it's a kind of graded scale. I did not say that at the end of the scale the photographs of faces only is inferior, is not to be accepted. I only said this sort of a graded scale, but I've also said that although the message with the best diagnostic value also have some disadvantage, like it's very difficult to organise, it's much easier and you can in fact do many more of those procedures if you can use photographs. So in fact I have never recommended and I don't think you can find that in my publications that you should not use photographs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in fact, let's look -- if we could look at page 43 of "Identifying Ivan" and you say -- you're talking about different options and you say: "Another factor was presentation by stills, video, or live line-ups," and then you go on to say: "The difference between the recognition rates in these conditions was marginal or non-existent." Do you still hold that view today?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah, marginal in the sense that the diagnostic value of -- and all of my own work, all my studies, are done with photographs of faces. I have obtained very high diagnostic values. So there's simply no way I could say that photographs are not good enough, if used properly. I'm not saying that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: So if that's the point of this discussion, yes, photographs are, if used in the proper manner, perfectly acceptable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's move to paragraph 21, the -- what if the rules are violated. And if we could look at page 83 of the -- no, I'm sorry, it's not 83. I'll have to -- if you could look at the Tadic transcript. Do you still have it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I could draw your attention to page 5779. And the question that's put to you, and I just want to see if you still agree with this position: "If I may proceed to Rule 49, should a breach of rules as we have been discussing so far," and just to pause for a moment, in Tadic you had 50 -- you talked about 50 rules in Tadic. Correct, Professor? In the Tadic --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Wait a minute. You are in line 7 of this page?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to pause for a minute because there's a reference to Rule 49 and I just want to clarify for the benefit of the Court that in Tadic --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: I'm not sure what this refers to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll get to this in a moment, in Tadic and in your book "Identifying Ivan" you have 50 rules; correct? And for the purposes of this case you've reduced them to ten rules. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. But on this page you're referring to me there's even mention of a Rule 52. So that cannot be the listing from the Ivan book.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: So that's why I'm saying I'm not exactly sure what this numbering refers to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it's possible that that's a typographical error. Don't worry about rule 52. Let's look at line 7, Rule 49 and I'll just go back to this question. "If I may proceed to Rule 49, should a breach of rules as we have been discussing so far were not justified in a written report lead to a rejection of identification in terms of quality of your field of expertise?" And your answer is: "There I might be invading, say, what is called the domain of the Court, I think, because it is not for me to reject any tests. So I know that rule is maybe not appropriate for an expert to express. But of course it contains a clear warning that there are cases in which rules were being breached to such an extent that really the logical impact of the recognition is totally absent. In that case, at least, I think it should be made known to the Court that there is a real problem. I do not want to express here that I would prescribe -- want to prescribe to the Court what to decide in such a case." I take it that you still agree with what you have expressed there in that case.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Of course I'm not prescribing the Court anything at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were asked on direct examination about what happens in England when -- if the Court finds a violation of the rules. Are you aware that -- just to pursue that point a little bit, are you aware that in England if there is a violation of the PACE rules, it is not -- the identification is not automatically thrown out, the Court evaluates all of the circumstances to decide whether the identification can still be received, whether it goes to weight, and so forth.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly the same things happens in the Netherlands where the Minister of Justice prescribes some rules. It's still for the Court whether to accept identifications.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The same is true in the United States, is it not? And this is expressed in a case which you discuss in your book, the Ivan book, Neils versus Biggers and it's later amplified in a decision called Manson. And in the United States if there's a breach of the rules, if there's a finding of suggestiveness in the procedure or in the photo spread, then what the Court does in deciding what to do with the identification is it essentially looks at the estimator variables. Is that correct? So it looks at things like the outward --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: I'm not an expert on American law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, this is a decision that you cited in your book, so I thought you were familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: But you describe -- you seem to describe a present practice and I'm not an expert on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: But I -- I think if you describe it that way, I can easily accept that interpretation of American law from you, but I'm not an expert.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. If Mr. Whiting is, and I think he is, is going to pursue this a little further, I say nothing about the American circumstance. I'm slightly concerned about the way he's left the English position with the witness at page 102, line 10/11. He's talking about the court's approach, looking at the circumstances to decide whether the identification can still be received, whether it goes to weight and so forth. That, in my understanding, with respect is not the position in England. The judge deciding on admissibility will decide on admissibility, taking into account any breaches he or she finds have taken place with regard to the procedures. If the judge finds the evidence admissibility, notwithstanding breaches, it is admissible. It would be a matter for the jury as to what weight it attached. So the judicial exercise that a judge is engaged upon in England has nothing whatever to do with weight. For once it is admissible, it is a matter for the fact-finder to decide what weight to attach to it. I say, I say nothing about the American experience. It's not within my sphere.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But I am sure, as Mr. Whiting knows, this is an issue in American law of admissibility, not an issue of weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, with respect to the English law, I was relying on a case Regina versus Forbes and it was my understanding, although I this is an area I am certainly not an expert, my understanding is if there was a violation of the rules and the court admitted the evidence, that the jury in some circumstances could be informed of the violation of the rules. That was what -- it is that I meant could go to weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Oh yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It was that that I meant could go to weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Absolutely. In assessing -- yes, it's -- it is Queen against Forbes in the House of Lords. In assessing what weight the fact-finder should give to the evidence, then the judge should direct the jury that he or she has found that there may have been breaches in the procedures and the jury must take those breaches into account when assessing weight. I was merely relating to the judge's exercise, not the once it gets beyond the judge and before the jury. Mr. Whiting is absolutely right, if that's what he meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's what I meant when I put the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any event, with respect to the Neils test, the court -- some of the things the court will look at, if there is a finding that suggestiveness has in fact occurred, not just the possibility of suggestiveness, but suggestiveness or bias has in fact occurred, the court will look at the opportunity of the witness to view the offender, the witness's degree of attention, the accuracy of the prior description, the degree of certainty, and the length of time between the crime and the identification procedure. Those are the factors that are set out. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Well, I must say, this discussion is a little bit beyond me. But the point I tried to make in section 21 is in fact two points. One is that a violation of the rules usually makes a test weaker, not stronger at all. In the end, you can have weakened the test so much that it doesn't prove anything anymore; that's all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I didn't want to get caught up in the niceties of the Neils decision. The point I was trying to put to you and see if you would agree with me is that if there is a problem -- put it broadly like that -- a problem with the system variables, it would be reasonable, would it not, for a court to consider the estimator variables in determining the weight and significance of that problem. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: No, no. Not generally. That might be informative also, but there are situations in which there is nothing wrong with the estimator variables. The witness had a perfect view long enough, there's no reason to doubt whether he remembers the culprit, but still with the system variables so much went wrong that he was led to the wrong response. That's still possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's possible. That's possible. What I'm asking is: If a court generally could get some confidence in evaluating problems with the system variables by taking into consideration, at least, the estimator variables.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: No. Maybe this is what you want to hear, but my opinion is that a court should always look at the estimator variables, and some estimator variables are necessary conditions for a good recognition but never sufficient conditions to explain the results of a test. Because even if there is no doubt in the mind of the witness what the culprit looked like, then still it's possible to direct this witness to a picture of a person -- of an innocent person. So estimator variables are necessary conditions; they're not sufficient conditions. You can never say: Since the estimator variables were good, we don't need the system variables anymore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I'm not suggesting that.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm suggesting, Professor, is that it's proper to consider in evaluating problems with the system variables the estimator variables. That could make a big deference in how you might look at a particular violation in a -- in system variables. You don't agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: No, I think it's the wrong way of putting it. It's always important for a court to look at the estimator variables, but it cannot -- in my mind, it cannot logically - I'm not talking about legally - but you cannot logically accept the results of a line-up test if the estimator variables are okay but the system variables are massively flawed. So yeah, my way of expressing it is: Of course a Court should always look at the system variables; that's extremely important. But you cannot let the one be a compensation for the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going back to Gary Wells, Gary Wells has written about -- and I provided you with the article. It's -- the article is: What's wrong with the Manson test.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he's written about some problems, and you don't need to look through it --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: That's a web site sort of article, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's an article that's on his web site. It's the same article that's cited in your report.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: I'm just trying to help me remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is the web site article and it's a draft of an article that he's writing.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if Mr. Younis could provide that. It's this article here.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: He again provides some rules, right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, he is talking about this test that we have just been talking about in the United States about if there's -- that's in the Neils test and it's also expressed in the Manson test that if there is a finding of suggestiveness then you look at the conditions of the identification to evaluate whether the identification is admissible. And -- he has some criticisms of the test and then he considers an alternative rule where if there is a finding of suggestiveness in the procedure, that the identification should, per se, be excluded. I just want to read what he says about that.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: It's about the referral.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see this has no page numbers. It is -- it's towards the end. It's on the page that has the words "final notes" at the very bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's about the referral of the proof. Right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it's -- yes, right. And on that page where it says "final notes" I'm just going to read the paragraph, the first full paragraph that starts there. He says: "However" -- and I just want to get your view on it after I've read it. "However appealing the per se exclusions might be at some levels it neglects the fact that there was a logic behind the court's holding in Manson that should be reserved. Consider, for instance, a case where we can be very sure that the eyewitness has a reliable memory. Perhaps it is an abduction case in which the victim eyewitness was held for days by the culprit. The culprit never wore a mask. There was good lighting. The culprit's face was in full view for hours at a time. And the witness was able to describe in detail the size, shape, and location of unique scars on the culprit's face. "Suppose now that a line-up was held only hours after the victim was rescued, but the line-up used unnecessarily suggestive procedures because the fillers did not fit the description of the culprit. Given the profoundly favourable circumstances of witnessing, would it be reasonable to suppress the identification merely because there were not good fillers for the line-up? There is an extreme example, but it illustrates a basic point. The court was correct in Manson to argue the issue of whether identification is nevertheless reliable in spite of the suggestiveness, per se exclusion based only on the finding of suggestiveness would not be in the interests of justice." Do you agree or disagree with that view expressed by Gary Wells?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: I disagree. I disagree with the initial stage where we say: "Let us assume," consider a hypothetical case, where he seems to argue that a case under such condition - saw the culprit for a long time, didn't wear a mask, and so on, saw the scars and everything - the witness simply cannot be wrong. That's the sort of assumption we are asked to make. The witness cannot be wrong. Now does it matter how we test such a witness? It seems to suggest that in cases of abduction, in longer abduction and in close proximity to the perpetrators, there never have been mistaken identifications. I can tell you, that is not so. I gave you the example of Valuse [phoen] from my book where the witnesses saw Mr. Valuse for more than a year and still they were demonstrably wrong. So the assumption here is not reasonable. So the assumption here that in such a condition the witness cannot be wrong is misleading; a witness can be wrong. And if there is no evidence, if you really needed identification evidence right? Because there is no evidence to link the witness to this abduction and everything really depends on the identification test, there's every reason to conform to the rules because you simply cannot argue that a mistake under such conditions is not humanly possible; it is. We know. And if you look at the list of -- say, the list of the 40 cases described by Gary Wells and others, some of them are about abductions and lots of things, as well it looks not unlike this and still there was a mistake. So --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: If the point of the test is that this evidence is essential for linking the suspects to a crime, then there is every reason to follow the rules.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just on that last point, you're not suggesting that any of the examples in those 40 cases, that you have any information that they were anything like this example.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: No, they might well be of that type. I have met myself many of those cases and I see no particular reason why none of them should be there. And in fact, in fact the acceptance of unsafe identification procedures is enhanced by some sort of belief that it doesn't matter because the suspect [sic] can't be wrong anyway. Suspects [sic] can be wrong in an incredible manner when it comes to identifying people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to those 40 cases, since you brought them up, you believe that in 30 cases there was just a single witness. A single witness in 30 of those 40 cases.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Well, the victims. They're called victims in that paper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: This is exactly the position he describes. It is the victim that is so certain that she can't be wrong.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM ALBERT WAGENAAR
utterances.text: Well, for that we have a test. Why shouldn't we run the test properly?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't have any further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I have no re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: As I understand it, no one else does either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They don't have the chance, perhaps. Professor, you will perhaps have discerned from that that counsel has lived up to their promise of trying to conclude your evidence today. We have reached the end of your questioning. The Chamber is grateful for your assistance and thanks you for being here today. You may leave and return to your other interests. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That brings us to the questions whether there are any other matters that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Just ever so briefly, I was reviewing the transcript and I believe it's page 109, line 25, I believe the Professor said "suspects" -- he said "suspects" can be wrong in an incredible manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Witnesses was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mine, too. Mine, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That probably means we're both wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Probably so, but I wouldn't want to identify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The question is whether the Chamber will need to sit later this week. That, I take it, closes the Defence case then?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honour, it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In all three facets.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, apart from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Some 92 bis potentially.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have three statements to put in rebuttal evidence. Two of the statements -- and they will be all 92 bis statements and they will be ready in 92 bis form tomorrow. The first two statements are agreed with the Defence; there's no dispute. The third, there is a dispute and the dispute is really with counsel for Mr. Limaj, and we've agreed, subject to the agreement of the Court, that we'll do that in writing. I can file a very brief motion explaining why we submit that it's proper rebuttal and Defence counsel can respond and then that can be considered. But that can all be filed this week. I would, finally, suggest that perhaps we set some kind of a deadline for all the 92 bis statements to come into evidence just so that it doesn't drift. I don't know what would be appropriate. There's no surprises, I think, but just so that it gets done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Does that mean that you agree, Mr. Whiting, that there is nothing more for the Chamber to need to hear in the form of oral evidence, rebuttal, or matters of that nature, and that whatever else needs to be done can be done in written form?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. And you would anticipate your written material being before the Chamber perhaps even tomorrow. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, tomorrow. The -- I can submit the two agreed rebuttal statements tomorrow and the -- and then I -- I'm quite confident I can submit the motion with the third contested rebuttal statement tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Khan, if that is done, will Friday be time enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: It will be. It is a short matter and focussing on what is rebuttal evidence and whether or not it ought to be heard at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Friday following, would that be time enough for your 92 bis formalities to be concluded?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, all the formalities, as I understand it, and perhaps the registrar can help, that need to be conducted by the Defence have been. You've been seized of some time, of course, in relation to the written motion. A formal request has gone to the registry. It's a matter for the registrar, as far as I understand it, to complete the administrative requirements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: As soon as it can. And, Your Honour, whenever the registrar is able to organise the logistics, the procedure can be carried out. Your Honour, of course, it's a matter for you. At first blush it doesn't seem necessary to impose time limits. I'm sure one can trust the registrar to discharge his responsibilities promptly in this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that Mr. Whiting may actually have a fourth rebuttal statement that he is not thinking through. It's been a matter of some argument back and forth, but in the case that does become an issue, we will have the matter taken care of within the week. He for sure has three; he may actually have a fourth which is in some discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm trying to give him some hope here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The question is: You have completed your procedures?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: My procedures are complete. We don't have a rejoinder case -- I notice you mentioned rebuttal but I wanted to make sure you were not contemplating a rejoinder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Topolski, there any matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes. I'm conscious of the time. I don't want to make life difficult for the defendants back at the UNDU. I'll be very brief. We have a number of 92 bis statements that are, as it were, down in Kosovo being approved by the witnesses. I had hoped to make an application on that well known piece of legislation, the Ways and Means Act to see if I could persuade this Chamber to be not so allied to 92 bis, but in light of what you said to Mr. Khan earlier on, I dare not go near that water because I felt its temperature already. Your Honour, in that sense we are in the hands of others. Your Honour appreciates it's now the registry and either somebody going down to Kosovo from here and complying with and completing the procedures. I would be very grateful if you please didn't tie me to a date that I would be honour bound to give you now and have this dealt with by then for fear that my position to comply is not entirely within my control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Does this mean that the procedures on your part have been completed?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: We are awaiting confirmation of the contents of some of the statements in Kosovo. So the straight answer to your question is as I speak now no. But I will ensure before I leave The Hague tomorrow, Wednesday, that it is, because I can direct those down there to do it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thereafter your position will be the same as Mr. Khan's?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: It will, except I'm slight reluctant to, as it were, step aside and let a date be given where I'm not in control of the process. I hope Your Honour follows what I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We were fixing a date for Mr. Khan so don't worry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: It would be on a best-endeavours basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What I want to be sure is that you reach a position in the next day or two in which it's merely for the registrar after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honour, that assurance I can give, that I will do all I can to ensure that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I do apologise. Your Honour, just one very brief matter before you and Your Honours rise. Your Honours may recollect that a while back Mr. Mansfield alluded to the fact that Mr. Churcher would be preparing a short addendum report in response to Mr. Clark's 92 bis witness statement. Your Honour, that addendum was filed this morning with the registry. I wonder for just the administrative purposes if that can be appended to DL13, which is the exhibit of Mr. Churcher's report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, that will be done. So it will become a further part of DL13. We should now break for the concerns that have been mentioned. The timetable ahead has been set and I believe is clear so we have no need to repeat that. Should there be any unforeseen difficulty with statements or submissions, an approach to the Chamber staff can facilitate a hearing at short notice. We will adjourn now until we complete the processes of written submissions and then the hearing of the final oral submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it follows, therefore, that we do not gather together again until the 20 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: End of August. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: We wish the Tribunal a pleasant summer break if it's to happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We are way off yet, but we are grateful. Yes. We hope you recover from your recent splendid news.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.08 p.m.
